speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: OLD AGE AND THE BLIND-CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement in regard to pensions for the aged and the blind.
As a result of negotiations with the provinces extending over several months, agreement has been reached on a number of changes in the administration of this scheme. I now wish to table two orders in council which have been passed implementing these changes. Before

Old Age and Blind Pensions
the new proposals become operative, a supplementary agreement must be entered into with each of the provinces. However, it is expected that in view of the provincial agreement to the substance of these changes, there will be no delay in the execution of these agreements. The effective date of their coming into force will be April 1, 1944, or such later date in the case of any province as may be desired by that province.
The most important change increases the amount of allowable outside income which a pensioner may have. When the maximum amount of pension \vas increased in 1943 from $240 to $300 a year, the maximum total income which a pensioner could have from all sources was allowed to remain at $365 a year. The allowable income from sources other than old age pension was therefore reduced from $125 to $65 a year. With the consent of the provinces, we are now providing for an increase in the maximum income which a pensioner may receive from $365 to $425 a year. In other words, the pensioner will be allowed other income of $125 a year instead of $65 a year, without a reduction in the amount of his pension. The maximum income allowed blind pensioners will also be increased by the amount of $60 a year.
While the amendment will not increase the maximum pension of $300 a year, it will benefit pensioners with small incomes who could not previously qualify for the increase in pension granted in 1943. Those who are now receiving an old age pension at the maximum rate of $25 a month would not be entitled to receive an increase in the amount of their pension, unless by way of supplemental allowances which are now being paid in certain provinces.
Other amendments are intended to meet as far as may be practicable under the present law the difficulties arising out of the residence qualifications. Certain of the existing regulations were causing disappointment and difficulty for pension applicants who for various reasons had been outside of Canada for extended periods or had found it necessary to transfer their residence from one part of Canada to another. One proposed change will enable an applicant who failed to qualify with the sixteen years' residence requirement between the ages of fifty and seventy, in the case of an applicant for an old age pension, and between the ages of twenty and forty in the case of an applicant for a blind pension, to make up the deficiency by a further period of residence in Canada equal to the deficiency. Under the old regulations in some extreme cases he might have had to wait sixteen full years following his return to Canada before
he qualified for a pension. Another proposed change will eliminate the necessity of an applicant who has recently moved to a new province returning to the province of previous residence for the sole purpose of applying for a pension.
Other cases of difficulty with regard to the residence requirement were found in instances of temporary absence from Canada as a result of service on ships or in fishing. The new regulation will permit such periods of temporary absence to count as residence in Canada provided the applicant maintained a self-contained domestic establishment in Canada during such periods.
Some weeks ago the house was advised that although there had been in the past certain legal doubt as to whether the clause relating to recoveries from estates of deceased pensioners was mandatory or permissive in its effect, the dominion in accordance with later -legal advice had indicated to the provincial pension authorities that whether or not recovery should be made from estates where the net value does not exceed $2,000 would be left entirely to their discretion.
These changes represent the result of a very careful examination of the steps which the dominion would recommend to make the present legislation meet the immediate practical problems without radical revision of the whole scheme.
As the house will recall, the speech from the throne stated that the working out of a comprehensive national scheme of social security, in which federal and provincial activities will be integrated, will require further consultation and close cooperation with the provinces and indicated that the government would be prepared "when suitable agreements are reached with the provinces," to recommend a measure for a national scheme of contributory old age pensions on a more generous basis than that at present in operation.
The adoption of a national scheme of contributory old age pensions would involve a fundamental revision of our old age pension legislation. This must, of necessity, await the holding of the dominion-provincial conference.
In adopting a contributory system it will, in my opinion, be found advisable not only to increase the scale of pensions but to reduce the eligible age and to have the pensions paid as a matter of right rather than on the basis of a means test, which is an essential feature of the present scheme and the cause of most of its administrative difficulties.
Certain of the provinces would be agreeable to lowering the eligible age from seventy to sixty-five years immediately for the non-con-
Old Age and Blind Pensions

tributary pensions being paid under the present scheme. It is, however, very doubtful whether it would be possible to obtain the agreement of all the provinces to such a reduction of the eligible age under the present scheme, as this would be a very far-reaching change involving a substantial increase in the financial and administrative burdens upon the provinces. If nevertheless, all or substantially all the provinces should make representations to the dominion government in favour of lowering the eligible age from seventy to sixty-five years under the present scheme, I can assure the house that the government will be prepared to give consideration to the acceptance of such representations as an interim measure in anticipation of and pending discussions with the provinces regarding a contributory scheme.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING GOVERNMENT MARKETING AND PRICE POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 27 I reported to the house that the basis of wheat marketings for the 1944-45 crop year would have to be determined at a later date, when account could be taken of the development of the 1944-45 crop, the probable export and domestic demand, and the elevator space and transportation available for handling the 1944-45 grain crops. The government will be in a much better position in July to appraise these factors bearing on the need for delivery quotas and an over-all limitation on wheat deliveries from the 1944 crop. For the balance of the 1943-44 crop year, however, I wish to announce that the eighteen-bushel limitation per authorized acre will be removed forthwith.
In the spring of 1941 owing to lack of available storage and restricted export demand, the policy of limiting deliveries to estimated export and domestic demand for the ensuing crop year was instituted. This policy meant, in effect, that the dominion government would permit marketings of that quantity of wheat which could be disposed of within the crop year. In 1941-42 the limitation was set at 230,000,000 bushels for all of Canada; in 194243 the limitation was 280,000,000 bushels for the west, and for the present crop year 1943-44 deliveries in the west were first limited to fourteen bushels per authorized acre; later this figure was increased to eighteen bushels per authorized acre.

Grain Marketing and Price Policy
As members of the house know, during the past year the demand for Canadian wheat, both at home and abroad, has increased substantially. To date in the present crop year, commercial disappearance of Canadian wheat has amounted to about 350,000,000 bushels, as compared with 213,000,000 bushels for the same period last year. We conservatively estimate that commercial disappearance of Canadian wheat for the crop year 1943-44 will amount to 425,000,000 bushels, as compared with 270,000,000 bushels during 1942-43. From August 1, 1943, to May 19, 1944, producers in the prairie provinces marketed 230,000,000 bushels of wheat, or 120,000,000 bushels less than commercial demand for Canadian wheat during the crop year to date.
The Canadian wheat board carefully surveyed remaining farm stocks in the prairie provinces and estimate that producers will market about 265,000,000 bushels of wheat under the eighteen-bushel limitation, and about 305,000,000 bushels if the restriction on deliveries is removed for the balance of the crop year. In other words, with the restriction on deliveries removed for the balance of the crop year, marketings during the present crop year will still remain about 120,000,000 bushels less than commercial disappearance for the crop year.
Available storage space in country elevators has been increasing rapidly in recent months, and at the present time there is over 100,000,000 bushels of space available for the immediate delivery of grain in the three prairie provinces, and grain is being shipped out of country elevators at a rapid rate.
The government's decision removing the restriction on the marketing of wheat for the balance of the crop year is therefore based upon a careful appraisal of domestic and export demand and the storage situation which now exists in western Canada.

PRICES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to ask leave of the house to move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) the adjournment of the house to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance namely, that the price set for strawberries in British Columbia by administration order A-1224,
3308	COMMONS
Strawberries-Prices in British Columbia
effective to-day, is so low that the farmers are unable to pick their berries and the crop is therefore going to waste.

subtopic: PRICES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
The hon. member has
given me a statement of the reasons why he asks leave to move the adjournment of the house. I find that there is a degree of urgency* The hon. member for Fraser Valley moves, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) for leave to adjourn the house on the grounds stated by him. Is it the pleasure of the house that the hon. member shall have leave to move the adjournment of the house?
And leave having been granted:

subtopic: PRICES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
First of all I should like to point out that this does not concern just my riding; it concerns the whole province of British Columbia. It just happens that most of the berries and small fruits generally are in my riding.
I should like to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the minister that the berry growers in my riding are not by any manner of means complaining of the action of the wartime prices and trade board in trying to control the cost of production and inflation; but we are emphatic in our opinion that deflation is far more important than inflation. While we approve the idea of controlling inflation, we certainly ask the minister to protect us as berry growers . from the deflation which we think will result from the board's order.
For the benefit of hon. members who are not familiar with small fruit growing I might explain that in the first place the land has to be of high quality, that it has to be very intensely cultivated and well and properly fertilized to get anything like a decent crop. In the province of British Columbia we arg faced with a higher original cost for our land, with higher taxes on that class of land than in any other part of the country, and with higher wages in connection with all branches of berry growing or other small fruit production. I presume hon. members are familiar with the figures set out in the order which goes into effect to-day.

subtopic: PRICES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: What are they?

subtopic: PRICES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I will answer that question in a moment. I am moving the adjournment of the house to-day because I think it is quite obvious to every hon. member of the house that in connection with a perishable fruit of any kind, if remedial action is to be taken that must be done at once.
With respect to the order, the dominion is divided into three zones for the purposes of

the price ceiling. Ontario and Quebec are in zone 1, the maritimes are in zone 2, and British Columbia is in zone 3. Incidentally the figures for the maritimes are the same as those for British Columbia, so that I need only give the figures for Ontario and Quebec and British Columbia. Effective as of to-day the maximum price in zone 3 is 27 cents a quart, or 144 cents a pint-and I would point out to the house that in my province we deal in pints rather than quarts. That is the maximum price to the producer. For the same period the price to the consumer is set at 39 cents a quart or 22 cents a pint. After June 17 the farmer in British Columbia will be allowed only 12 cents a pint. We cannot possibly produce berries in my province at that rate. I do not want to weary the house any more than is necessary, but this is a matter of vital importance not only to the farmers but to the whole economic structure of British Columbia.
Incidentally I should like to say a word about deflation. This government has been very proud of what it has done under the Veterans' Land Act, about which I shall have something to say later; they are proud of what is to be done for the veterans when they come home. We have taken over some 750 Japanese farms in the province of British Columbia, which are being held for our veterans. All these farms were devoted to the production of berries prior to the evacuation of the Japanese, and no soldier can carry on at deflated prices. No member from British Columbia has been consulted, nor to the best of my knowledge has any organization of producers in that province been consulted by the board in arriving at these figures. In fairness to the board I must say that I think they want to do the right thing, as I know the minister wants to do the right thing for the farmers of British Columbia and every other part of Canada, but I do not think a sufficiently thorough study of the problem was made before setting the figures at which we are expected to produce.

subtopic: PRICES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: What prices are you suggesting?

subtopic: PRICES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I shall come to that in a moment, and will carry New Brunswick with me, if my hon. friend will give me time. In 1943 the cost of production in British Columbia was 12-57 cents a pound, but effective as of to-day we are allowed only 14J cents a pound and after June 17 will be allowed only 12 cents. In the eastern part of British Columbia berries will not come to production until after June 17. In the Fraser valley and the lower mainland they will commence to

Strawberries-Prices in British Columbia
come into production about June 10. The dominion and provincial governments are not even opening their pickers hostel at Haney, in the heart of the Fraser valley fruit district, until June 10; yet this order is put into effect as of May 29. In passing I want to say that the selling figures I am giving are not my estimates; I am quoting the figures given by the gentleman whom I understand is in charge of this matter, Mr. E. J. Chambers, the administrator of fresh fruits and vegetables for the wartime prices and trade board. The production figures were prepared by a large berry cooperative.

subtopic: PRICES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Mr. Chambers is from British Columbia.

subtopic: PRICES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Yes, and he is a very fine man, as are all men who come from British Columbia. In arriving at his figures he refers to the years 1938, 1939, 1940, and 1941. The approximate average for those four years, at the shipping point, was slightly over $1.60 per crate. I want the farmer members of this house, particularly, to think of that. This gentleman is basing the prices he is setting in the year 1944, with present cost of production, on the prices received by the Japanese farmers in the province of British Columbia. How can anyone expect a white farmer to operate under similar conditions? I do not say that the Japanese received enough; I know they did not, according to the figures given by the board. Again these are not my figures; they are quoted by the wartime prices and trade board. In 1941 the average price of berries per quart in the province of British Columbia was 8-9 cents. Can you imagine that?-8-9 cents for a quart of berries. In 1942 the price was 12 cents; in 1943 it was 33 cents, yet this year we are asked to produce for a maximum of 27 cents, though when we can get it we are paying hoeing labour 50 to 65 cents an hour. Last Saturday right in this city berries were selling at 59 cents a quart or 30 cents a pint.

subtopic: PRICES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: They are imported.

subtopic: PRICES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I do not care
where they come from. I am getting a good deal of assistance from the hon. member for York-Sunbury, for which I am grateful. While berries are being imported and sold at this rate, we are not shipping. I wonder if any member of the wartime prices and trade board or any member of this house ever saw them picking strawberries for the first shipments. Why, in a field of strawberries the size of this room you would be extremely
lucky to get two crates of berries. That is no exaggeration; in order to get our berries [DOT]to that early market they have to be picked here, there and everywhere throughout the field, because only a few are ripe and in condition.
Another thing to be kept in mind is that unfortunately in British Columbia we are not heavily industrialized and do not have the large early market. We ship our berries largely to the prairie provinces, and in order to ship them over the mountains you must pick the berries at a certain stage and under certain weather conditions or they will not stand the trip. Apparently some people have the idea that we just turn the pickers loose with pails, but that is not the way they are picked in British Columbia. The berries must be sorted, graded and packed, and that all costs money. I presume it is the same in other parts of Canada, but I am speaking from my knowledge of British Columbia.
How they arrived at these prices, I do not know, but from their own statement they have used as a basis the average for the four years I mentioned. They also based it, as I understand it-and again there was no statement-on the assumption that they expected twenty per cent of our berries would be shipped by crate. I know, and every farmer member knows - probably there are some others who are not so familiar with the country-that we make our profits on crated berries, shipped to the higher priced market. This year, according to their own figures, the board states we will get an average of $3 a crate. They are working on the assumption, again according to their own statement, that we begin shipping on May 29-to-day. In eastern British Columbia they do not start until after the seventeenth, and in other parts until the twentieth. I do not blame the board for that, because no man alive can predict when we will ship, or how many we will ship, because the Lord Almighty attends to that. It is a perishable product, as we all know. But they base their price upon $2.88 as a maximum, and a rate of 12 cents a pint is allowed. There is a maximum amount of 14J cents a pint. They base their average of $3, according to their statement, on the assumption that the farmer will ship on May 29. Well, we are not by any means starting to ship at that time. They also base their average of $3 on the assumption that we are going to ship twenty per cent by crate. The actual facts are that 'last year the largest strawberry shippers in British Columbia shipped out of one of their freight centres exactly ten per cent in crates and ninety per cent in jam. Yet these

3310	COMMONS
Strawberries-Prices in British Columbia
geniuses down here in Ottawa can tell us that we are going to ship twenty per cent by crate, starting to-day, when the berries are not even ripe. That is the position they take, when actually last year we shipped only ten per cent. As hon. members know, when the berries are made into jam you get a very low price.
Last year the average cost of pickers in British Columbia was four cents a pint. That is the way we pay our pickers out there. We pay a basic rate of four cents, and a bonus for staying the whole season. I assume that that is done in other areas of Canada as well. Last year the average cost of production in British Columbia was 12-57 cents per pound. These figures are taken from the records of over 800 berry producers, and they have been averaged over that number. Therefore the figure I have given is last year's average cost. And mark this: I presume everyone know's that the average life of the strawberry plant is five years. In the first year they are planted there is no return to the farmer at all. Then, if you take in the cost of planting, cultivating, fertilizing, thinning, and all the other costs for the first year; hold off any allowance for rental of land, taxes, and add to that the cost of cultivating in the second year, it will be found that the average cost is 9-20 cents per pint. The maximum we are allowed at the rate set to-day is 12 cents.
I could give all sorts of statistics with respect to jam. However, I am prepared to prove my point before the board or anywhere else. I would like to point out that I, as a member for Fraser Valley, along with other members from British Columbia have been pressing this point since early in February. We have been insisting, in the first instance, that if a ceiling was to be placed on the berries we would oppose the ceiling, and I surely think it would be clear why we cannot have a ceiling on perishable goods such as strawberries which must be shipped across the mountains. If we had thought we were getting nowhere in preventing a ceiling being placed on berries, and that we would have had to wait until May 23 to have a ceiling announced, I wish to assure the minister he would not have had a solitary berry planted in the Fraser valley this year. Those berries would not have been planted if we had known that we had to sell them at 12 cents a pint or in other words, pay the consumer for consuming them.
I know it may be said that the board sets all these orders. I can understand perfectly well that if any branch of the government, or

any person connected with it, makes a mistake, the minister must assume responsibility for that mistake. In the long run the Prime Minister has to assume the responsibility for the mistakes of his ministers, and, to carry it even further, parliament has to look after the mistakes made by the Prime Minister and his government. I can see no earthly reason why any argument should be advanced against the minister's overruling the wartime prices and trade board. They are doing a very difficult job and, I believe in most cases, the board are doing very well. I give them credit for it. But I do say that when an injustice is being done it is the minister's duty to overrule.
I could give a typical example, in connection with banking. This matter came up before a committee which sits in another room in this building. They were-

subtopic: PRICES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Order; the hon. member should not make reference to that committee.

subtopic: PRICES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I withdraw that remark, Mr. Speaker. Then, I would ask the minister-and I believe I have ample support -to give further consideration to this matter. In conclusion I would point out that it is proper to criticize the minister or his department, if one has any suggestion to offer. We who represent the berry growers of the lower mainland-and I believe there are three members who are in that position-met the minister last Friday and made a suggestion to him. We thought we had made a reasonable suggestion, namely, that the dates of the various rates be retarded, a procedure which would have avoided upsetting the whole price structure that has been developed. In other words the rates would be held in abeyance. I am speaking from memory, but I think we suggested that the order be held in abeyance until June 15. It will go into effect to-day, but should be held in abeyance until that date at least. From June 15 to June 27 the rate would be 14J cents, I believe it was, and from there on it would be 12^ cents. In other words we offered a compromise.' We do not wish to make fortunes out of the berry crop, but on the other hand we do not want our farmers to be forced out of existence.

subtopic: PRICES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this occasion I speak more as a British Columbia member than as a member representing berry farmers. I have one small district in my constituency in which strawberries are grown. However this is a matter which affects a very large number of the berry farmers in British Columbia. I share an office with the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) and since

Strawberries-Prices in British Columbia
last February I have been hearing about berries. Hon. members in the house have heard the hon. member for Fraser Valley repeatedly ask whether a ceiling price would be set on berries.
My first criticism as a British Columbia member is that if a ceiling was to be placed on the price of berries, there is no reason why it should not have been done two months ago. In this instance there is a no D-day, and no element of surprise is necessary. The farmers were entitled to know two months ago what their prices would be. They should have known two months before the ceiling was put on. As my hon. friend has said, they would not have planted strawberries if they had known they were going to be given 12 cents a pint, in view of the fact that last year their basic cost was 12-52 cents. It would appear that when the ceiling price was set, it was not set on last year's price, but rather on prices from 1938 to 1942. It must be remembered that in that period of time the great bulk of berry farmers in British Columbia were Japanese. Japanese produced berries at prices at which no white man could ever attempt to produce them. They worked from dawn to dusk for ten and eleven cents an hour as their basic rate of pay. To-day the berry farmers of British Columbia-when they can get labour- must pay 65 cents an hour.
I do not think the people of British Columbia are objecting to price control, but they are objecting to our farmers being legislated into bankruptcy by the action of the wartime prices and trade board. There was no consultation with any of the berry-growing group in British Columbia. Certainly no British Columbia member was tipped off or asked in advance what he thought of these prices. These men of the prices board sit in their ivory tower down here, suddenly set a price and say, "You can like it or lump it." Well, we are not going to like it or lump it. Before the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) replies, there are one or two observations I should like to make on this particular order. I understand that there were no ceilings on strawberries last year. Strawberries are hardly a commodity that enter at this time of the year into the category of necessities of life, yet they probably do add something to the joy of life. Certainly I have had a great deal of difficulty in finding out in the last year's proceedings where the wartime prices and trade board have ever added anything to the joy of Canadian life since they were brought into being; and this is a splendid instance of that board, apart from the purpose of its necessary and essential duty, becoming a board of interference, a board that has destroyed its real value by its indifference to moving into the realm of nuisance value. It is high time that some supervising authority stepped in to prevent that board from destroying its own usefulness by its own folly and its own nonsense.
Everybody will agree that in war time prices should) be controlled. Everybody will agree that production should be regulated and that the distribution of things essential to a war time economy should be done with equity and fairness. I go farther than a great many of my hon. friends on this side of the house in believing firmly that in the economy of a power age the control and regulation of reasonable prices, of reasonable services, of reasonable production and distribution, is an essential part of our whole system of planned and organized life which we cannot escape. Here you find a typical example of the sort of thing that emanates only from unbridled bureaucracy. This is one of the dangers with which our whole peace-time programme is confronted, and one of the things that has hindered rather than helped our war effort.
Now let me just give a few examples of the sort of thing involved in this order. The zones are described; No. 1 takes in Ontario and Quebec, that section of the Dominion of Canada which has been favoured so long by this canoe-minded atmosphere in Ottawa.

speechtext:
I have never known any of you to suffer; and in any deal between central Canada and either the west or the east I notice that -central Canada always comes out on top. Let us look at this particular example, even in connection with a small thing like

strawberries. In zone No. 1, Ontario and Quebec, the strawberry grower receives 30 cents. In zone No. 2, the maritime provinces, the price drops to 27 cents, and in zone No.
3, British Columbia, the price is also down to 27 cents. Tell me why a strawberry grower in Ontario, with the 'huge market in this area, should get more at this season of the year than a grower in the maritime provinces or in British Columbia. The growers in central Canada have cheaper land; they have a better market, and they have cheaper labour. That is one situation. But let us see what happens when the table is turned, when they are packing their surplus in this area to compete with those who pack berries in the mari-times and British Columbia. Strangely enough the central packer again gets the benefit. After June 24 the price in Ontario and Quebec drops to 19 cents, while in the maritimes and British Columbia it is held at 22 cents. Let me ask this question. When conditions are in favour of the grower; when prices are high, with the new production coming on the market, why does the eastern producer benefit to the extent of three cents a quart; then, when it comes to producing for packing house competition with British Columbia and the maritime provinces, why should we find the central packer paying a price of 19 cents as against 22 cents which must be paid by the packer in British Columbia and the maritimes?
I know the Minister of Finance resents any criticism of the wartime prices and trade board, and I know that this board does not welcome suggestions from members of parliament. Under our modern bureaucracy we have been relegated to the background to the extent that it is an insult to our wartime prices and trade board, and to our bureaucrats, to dare offer a suggestion as the representatives of the people. I do not want anyone to accuse me of speaking for votes on this matter, because I do not happen to have any strawberry growers in my riding, and I suppose running true to human nature most of my constituents would like to get strawberries even in the early season just as Cheaply as possible. Apart from that, however, from long experience in British Columbia I know that all the people of that province will resent the idea of an unfair discrimination against the growers of British Columbia and the maritimes, and an unfair preference to the growers of central Canada. When a government undertakes to move into the discreet level above which profits may be made, or to dictate the discreet line along which any business must operate, that government will find that in doing so it is doing more harm
than good. If ceilings are to be fixed and floors established, they can be levelled out; it can be arranged upon a basis under which a reasonable amount of competition can exist between the floor and the ceiling. What we want to prevent in war time as in peace time is the unreasonable exploitation of the consumer in the consumers' market. We never want to undertake to restrict competition or to destroy the incentive of a reasonable and fair reward.
This, Mr. Speaker, is a splendid example of the need for reform in the wartime prices and trade board. It is typical of the harsh and arbitrary measures that are too often adopted by this board without the necessary experience to qualify them to dictate the policy and programme of the many businesses and of the farmers and producers upon whom they have fastened like a straitjacket an army of regulations and controls that now need revision, and many of which should be done away with. I congratulate the hon. member for Fraser Valley on bringing this matter to the attention of parliament, and I hope the minister responsible for this order will see that the kind of inequality, the kind of discrimination, the kind of preference and the kind of sectional differences that appear here are eliminated.

subtopic: PRICES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I believe the principles involved in this discussion are sound. I refer first to the principle of home production. It is my belief that to the greatest possible degree the Dominion of Canada should produce its own needs and should consume its own production. That applies to strawberries as well as to other commodities. The berry growers deserve, and in the interests of Canadian consumers must receive, prices covering costs of production and plus a fair remuneration. At the same time consumers must be protected; otherwise they will cease to use Canadian berries and will seek substitutes of one kind or another, again to the disadvantage of Canadian producers.
I should like to know upon what basis the wartime prices and trade board were working when they fixed the price of strawberries. I do not happen to be familiar with production of strawberries, and therefore I am not in a position to speak with any degree of authority in the matter. But it would be interesting to find out just how they computed the price. How did they determine what it ought to be? I am inclined to say, with respect to the wartime prices and trade board, that they have endeavoured to be fair to consumers. I believe their difficulty has arisen out of that desire, and I do not find too much fault with them, because I believe I understand their difficulty. Now they have endeavoured to fix a price which the consumer can, will and ought to pay. I believe that is right, and I believe the board are entitled to have a member say that. But at the same time the price upon which they have fixed is, it appears, one unquestionably lower than the grower can accept, or at which he can grow berries. What is going to be done about it? No one has thus far in the debate offered any suggestion as to what should be done. May I offer one? The solution of the difficulty will be found in a well-placed subsidy. There will be those who will say immediately that the principle of subsidies, being too expensive, is unsound. There will be no serious objection to the subsidy once it is realized that it can be paid out of the national credit, in so far as the goods and services producing and consuming capacity of Canada will justify the use of that credit. Just as soon as that principle is recognized it will be possible to pay a price which is fair to the producer and at the same time fair to the consumer. If a subsidy is necessary to bridge the gap between the two, then let a subsidy be paid.
Already we are using the principle of paying subsidies, in respect of many commodities. It

will do no harm to extend it. I believe it was last year, when the Minister of Finance was discussing the amount of money to be spent for the board which has to do with the adjustment of prices, that I pointed out I had only one fault to find with the appropriatoin, and that was that it was too small. I advocated something like $500,000,000 whereas the minister was asking for about $200,000,000-and I am speaking entirely from memory. Many hon. members thought I was extravagant, but I was not extravagant. If the economy of this country is to be established on a basis equitable and advantageous to all the people, both producers and consumers, a far more extensive use of subsidies must be made, so as to bring down prices to the consumers and bring them up for the producers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the discussion this afternoon must have brought home to all members of the house, and to all members of the public who are taking an interest in the matter, the difficulty of price control. The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) made a rather moderate request. He with some other British Columbia members made the request last Friday afternoon. I took it up with the wartime prices and trade board, where it was fully discussed, and eventually determined to be impracticable-or, if not impracticable, undesirable.
But before I come to that, let us consider this matter in its other aspects. A year ago, in the spring and summer of 1943, fruits and vegetables went to very high prices in this country, and we had from all parts of the country complaints that our much vaunted price ceiling, as it was called, was no price ceiling at all. It was said that while ,we held down the price of bread, the price of butter, the price of meat, and the price of some other necessities of life, we were not bringing about a realistic cost of living for Canada at all, because we were allowing fruits and vegetables, and a great variety of foods which most Canadians are able to buy to go uncontrolled. And so we felt we had to bring a great range of commodities under control this year which were not under control last year. In that list was fruit. That is the reason for a price ceiling on strawberries, along with a great many other fruits which were not controlled last year. We have not heard much from the consumer in this house at all. We do not hear that until we do something against the interests of consumers. For instance, let me take as an example the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair). He stands up in his place this afternoon and expresses sympathy with the hon. member for Fraser Valley when that hon.

Strawberries-Prices in British Columbia
member asks the government to let the price of strawberries go up. But last year, owing to the fact that we had let the price of a good many foods go up, during the first two months of the operation of the price ceiling it was found necessary to allow the price of meals in restaurants to be increased somewhat, and to permit an increased charge for tea and coffee. And the first member in this house to get up and launch an attack upon the government far its failure to control prices of foods, was the hon. member for Battle River. Members cannot have it both ways.
The hon. member for Yancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) also spoke this afternoon about prices. He talks half the time for the farmer and half the time for the packer. First he says how unfair it is to the farmers of eastern Canada and western Canada to allow a higher price ceiling for farmers in Ontario and Quebec during the early part of the season. "Why," he says, "they are held to 27 cents in the maritime provinces and also to 27 cents in British Columbia during the early part of the season. But look at Ontario and Quebec, the part of Canada which always gets the best of everything, and gets the best of the other provinces. They are not held down to 27 cents; they are allowed 30 cents." Then he said, "After they get into midseason see what they cutely do, to help Ontario and Quebec. What they cutely do then is to get the ceiling down to 19 cents in Ontario and Quebec, and allow the farmers to go up to 22 cents in the west and the maritime provinces." Now, he cannot have it both ways either.

If we were to allow the foreign product to go uncontrolled and controlled the domestic product, we would hear all kinds of inflammatory talk about bureaucracies-we have heard a lot of it this afternoon-and all this foolishness about bureaucrats and that sort of thing. In 1943 what was the situation in British Columbia? British Columbia's crop was only one-quarter of normal and prices rose to inflationary levels, being more than four times the prices which prevailed in 1940 and 1941, and more than two and a half times the prices of 1942. Let me give the production to show that what I am saying about shortages in the crop is true. In British Columbia the number of quarts produced in 1939 was 10,877,000; in 1940, 9,078,000; in 1941, 10,431,000; in 1942, 5,649,000; in 1943, 2,523,000. That shows the tremendous drop in production, and there was a tremendous rise in price. The price in British Columbia in 1943 did rise on the average to 33 cents a quart, and as I said before, that was four times the prices which prevailed in 1940 and 1941, and more than two and a half times the prices of 1942. In fixing a ceiling for 1944 I do not think it would be reasonable to take the conditions of last year, which were entirely extraordinary. The 1944 average ceiling is 9 or 10 cents a quart below the 1943 price but it is nearly double the 1942 price-not nearly double the old prices of 1938, 1939 and 1940, but nearly double the 1942 price. The 1944 ceilings do not constitute a roll-back on 1943 prices in other provinces and in each case are about double the 1942 prices.

Prior to October 1, 1942, orders in council of general or widespread interest or concern were published in eight volumes under the general title "Proclamations and Orders in Council relating to the War". Other orders in council relating, for example, to foreign exchange control, defence of Canada regulations, et cetera, were published from time to time in separate volumes.

Questions
The statutory orders and regulations order 1942 (P.C. 7992, September 4, 1942) provided for the publication by the privy council office in "Canadian War Orders and Regulations" of all orders in council relating to the war, of a legislative character or imposing a penalty. Since October 12 of that year "Canadian War Orders and Regulations" has appeared weekly.
Orders in council required by statute to be published in the Canada Gazette are printed from time to time in that publication.
Orders in council which have not been published or made public, since the beginning of the war, fall into two categories, namely:
(1)	Orders of a purely administrative character and of no general interest.
Such orders include those originating in the Department of Munitions and Supply, for the authorization of contracts between the Minister and manufacturers and suppliers of weapons and war supplies of all kinds. For this purpose the authority of the governor in council is required under the Department of Munitions and Supply Act. These account for approximately 70 per cent of all orders in council passed since the beginning of the war.
Also included in this category are those authorizing contracts by the Department of Public Works, appointments to various administrative positions and miscellaneous routine orders passed under the authority of various statutes.
(2)	Orders in council, the publication of which is withheld for security reasons.
In this category are included orders in council, the publication of which is omitted or deferred under the authority of the secret documents (non-publication) order 1941 (P.C. 5135 of July 15, 1941); the publication of such orders would otherwise be necessary. Also included within this category is a small number of orders in council in respect of which military authorities issue a certificate to the effect that their publication would convey information likely to be of value to the enemy. Such orders, for example, authorize military establishments and the like.

speechtext:
This is an important item. It concerns one of the two legislative bodies of this parliament. We hear complaints that the senate is not being given the importance that it has in our constitution. It is easy to make a comparison between our senate and the senate of the United States. Across the border the senate has much more importance than congress and it is because the American senators assumed the initiative on many important matters of public administration. There is an external affairs committee of the United States senate which decides the foreign policy of that country. They play a role of major importance, and I do not see why a discussion of matters which are so vital to our national life are left to the parliamentary assistant to the chairman of the privy council, the Prime Minister, who delivers broadcasts twice a week about matters that should be studied by a committee of the senate. I very seldom listen to the radio, but I should like to read the reports of such committees of the senate.
There are also other things that should be studied by the senate. Many conservative senators have died; let them rest in peace, but those who are still alive, though their party is dead, should meet together to discuss the vital questions of bureaucracy. They should study the civil service. On two occasions special committees of this house have recommended unanimously that a standing committee on the civil service should be set up. The government did nothing about it, but on the other hand there is in the senate a standing committee on the civil service, which never sits. It is in the same class as the honorary committee on debates, the same as the committee on public accounts which was sleeping until it was awakened by the present leader of the opposition. Yet those people complain that they are not sent any work by the House of Commons. They have completely lost any sense of shame in the senate, and with the exception of two or three senators for whom I have the deepest

Supply-Legislation-The Senate
admiration I concur in what was said by the leader of the C.C.F. party as to the abolition of that body. Here they are, sitting perhaps fifteen days or three weeks during the session. We can see what they do by looking at their Hansard; it is as thin as a sheet of tissue paper. They meet, shake hands and go away. They have nothing to do. If they were willing to work; if they had enough initiative, they could help us; they could play the part that was allotted to them under our constitution.
I am not surprised that the vacant seats are not filled by the government. I believe there are thirteen of them, which is quite a number. It is true that this government has a majority in the senate, but I remember the time when Mr. Bennett was in power and Mr. Sauve was Postmaster General. He was my political football at the time and I wanted to keep him in the house; I did not want the Prime Minister to appoint him to the senate. I told the right hon. gentleman what economy he was practising by not making appointments to the senate. He was saving $4,000 a year for each vacant seat, plus travelling expenses, and he found the idea so good that he kept the Postmaster General in the house, to my great enjoyment. But now it would be easy for the government to appoint good men to the senate, some of the members who vote with the government on all matters but do not say a word in the house, those for whom the Christmas tree is in full swing the year round. Someone was complaining that outsiders were appointed to the senate and that as a result members of parliament were suffering an injustice. I say it is a good thing that they received the treatment they deserved. They did nothing here, and the Prime Minister could not expect them to awaken in the senate after they had been sleeping in this house since the beginning of the war. The senate is a nonentity in our parliament at the present time, just on account of the unwillingness of the senators to do something while they are sitting there. It is a great honour to be in the senate; it is like a decoration for merit.

Exactly. And I have to say that what I have said is in order, and I will not speak of anything else. My contention is that it is my duty, my solemn duty, to establish to the satisfaction of the Chair that I have not infringed the rules of the house while I was speaking on this subject. And I do not want my words to be distorted by anybody. I never said that it was because a man had fat contracts that he had been appointed to the senate. My hon. friend said that. But I said that a man who had fat contracts had been appointed to the senate and had received a reward besides his contract. And this I can say, and it is not disrespectful to say it. It is not attacking the honourableness of the man, in the first place.
In the second place, if I say that the senate is an anachronism, there is absolutely nothing insulting about it. And I will take the dictionary to prove to you that the definition of "anachronism" has not anything at all disrespectful, or that is against the rules of the house. Moreover, I have the Concise Oxford dictionary from the table. This is the dictionary that is to give us the true significance of each word.
Anachronic: Involving anachronism; out of date.
Anachronism: Error in computing time; thing out of harmony with the present. So anachronistic.
In French, anachronisme. Is there anything against the rules of the house in using the word "anachronism"? Then, I used the word "nonentity." Well, when the senate does not sit, can we call the senate an entity? It is an entity, theoretically, but not in fact. At the present time the senate is not sitting. I can say it is a nonentity; they do not exist. Is there something that is disrespectful in mentioning those facts?
What did I say besides that? I said a gentleman had an important job with a big salary, while he was appointed to the senate- or before he was appointed to the senate. This is not disrespectful. I did not attack their character. He has no right to sue me for libel or slander if I say it in this house. Moreover, I can say it in the drawingroom of the princess; it is the king's language. And what did I say? I said that the other fellow had no political background. Is there something disrespectful about that? I take it, statement after statement, and there is positively nothing disrespectful in what I have said. On the other hand, if this committee of the whole has become a star chamber, I will not insist any more. But on the other hand, I ask the Minister of National Defence not to be so touchy.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, May 26, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war- Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
Export permit branch - administration, $153,805.
Could the minister make a general statement on these five or six items? This would facilitate our obtaining information when we come to deal with the particular items.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the suggestion of the hon. member is a good one. As a matter of fact I shall be glad to tell the committee something of the work going on in the department in connection with these various items under this war appropriation. I shall deal first with the export permit branch. This branch was established in the Department of Trade and Commerce in April, 1941. The purpose of export control is, first,
3332	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Trade and Commerce
to conserve materials for Canada's own requirements or those of her allies; second, to prevent exports going to dangerous destinations or undesirable consignees; third, to fulfil our commitments to the United Kingdom; fourth, to conserve supplies for Canadian civilian use and, fifth, to aid in the administration of United States export control and domestic policy and to prevent Canada from being used as a back door by persons wishing to evade United States export regulations.
This branch considers applications for permits to export and issues or refuses them after consultation with the various administrators and controllers. An interdepartmental committee on export control upon which are representatives of trade and commerce, munitions and supply, wartime prices and trade board and all other departments concerned, deals with special questions in regard to the issuance of export permits which present particular problems from the point of view of shortage of supply, allocation of exports to different markets, et cetera.
Subsidies are paid by the dominion government in order to maintain Canadian domestic price ceilings. These subsidies are not payable on goods for export. The export permit branch recovers any subsidy paid before issuing a permit. The amount of subsidies recovered from September 1, 1942, to April 30, 1944, was $407,998.81. This money was remitted, partly to the prices stabilization board and to the Department of Agriculture for dairy supplies. Export quotas have been set up for a number of commodities and this division supervises the allocation of them. A fee of $2 is charged for each permit to export, the value of which exceeds $100, and the revenue for the present fiscal year amounts to S174,394.91.

The minister has made a statement with regard to export permits and I notice that practically the same statement appears in his annual report. Could he give us the number of permits issued this year, not only for the exporting of general commodities but for the products of western Canada other than grain? I understand that his department controls the general export of everything, grain included. Perhaps the minister can give us the number of permits issued for the export of grain, to the United States in particular, and also the policy of the government with respect to the use of United States transportation facilities. As I understand it, a number of United States cars are sent direct to the western provinces and do not come under the same regulations that 	,
govern shipments by lake boats. Perhaps he can give us a little information about this.
Later on I shall have something to say about the different items. I notice that the auditor's report contains an item with respect to drawbacks received by the mills. The minister has said that subsidies are not paid on goods for export, but how about flour? I understand that a subsidy or a drawback is paid to the mills on wheat which is to be manufactured into flour, for both domestic and export use. How do they keep these apart? From the minister's statement I would gather that flour for export would not cany any subsidy or drawback, and I should like some information as to how the millers keep their accounts of these subsidies; how they keep track of the wheat used to produce domestic flour.
I think we should have an auditor's report as to the subsidies paid to the mills or whoever received it, also a statement as to the price paid for the grain delivered to the mills and the basis upon which the flour is sold. The other day a return was brought down by the minister's department giving the price of flour at Saint John, and on the basis of that return we find that the price of wheat figures out at more than a basis of $1.25 Fort William. This return was tabled on May 15 in reply to my request for prices of flour at Saint John and Vancouver. It shows that for mutual aid the price was $9.46 per 280 pounds. If you figure out how much wheat it takes to produce 280 pounds of flour you will find that they ought to have at least $1.50 for the wheat, taking it on the basis of forty-five pounds of flour from a bushel of wheat. Then there would be the middlings and bran and so on, which, according to the bureau of statistics, would figure at about twenty-seven cents. If we take these figures it comes to $1.77 for the wheat. How about the drawback which the miller gets? Is it the miller that gets it? If so, that amount would have to be added on top of the $1.77. What is the per bushel drawback, which would have to be added to the $1.77, including flour, middlings, bran and shorts on the minister's own basis of 280 pounds, Saint John, $9.40?

I am very anxious to give the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and any other hon. member all possible information on any of the items coming before the committee this afternoon. The item before us deals with export permits, and the hon. member is asking for information which is entirely foreign to the subject under discussion. Some of the information he has asked for could be given on my civil estimates. He has also asked for information as to

Fundy Air Lines
millers' drawbacks. That does not come under this department but under the Department of Finance.
The hon. member asked as to the number of export permits issued this year. The total number issued was 99,153. I am sorry I have not a break-down of these items, showing the commodities covered.
The hon. member also asked as to the use of United States cars for the movement of wheat. That does not in any way come under this item.
Does it not come under export?

It would not come under export permits, because export permits are not used in connection with that movement at all. The hon. member will have an opportunity to get that information on my civil estimates, when I shall be prepared to give it to him. I am not hesitating at all to give all the information available now, but I think it would facilitate the discussion if we confined ourselves to the item before us.
I know that a man has to have a permit to ship grain to the United States and that it would go there in some United States cars. I think my questions are quite pertinent therefore, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is this difficulty when there are both civil and war appropriation estimates. I think, however, it would shorten the discussion if the minister's suggestion were to be followed. He has stated that he has not the information before him that the hon. member desires.

I submit, Mr. Chairman, that my questions are pertinent, because according to the auditor general's report, page Y-6, after "Canadian shipping board administration" the next item that appears is "drawback claims for millers" and the next item is "export permit branch administration", and these items are all listed under the Department of Trade and Commerce. Further details are given on pages Y-25, Y-26, Y-27 and Y-28. I should like the figures of expenditures to compare them with the expenditures given in the auditor general's report for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1943, for "export permit branch administration".

The amount voted for 1943-44 was $144,160 for the export permit branch. This year we are asking for $153,805. The total expenditure for the fiscal year 1942-43 was $99,842.11, and for 1943-44, $136,851.78. The revenue for the
fiscal year 1942-43 was $139,727.53, and the revenue for 1943-44 was $174,394.81, showing that this branch operated at a profit of some $40,000 for the year.

The minister stated that the number of permits issued was 99,153. Quite a number of permits were refused last year according to the last annual statement. Would the minister state how many permits have been refused this year and to where the goods were consigned?
I have not that information before me at the moment.

Perhaps we could get it after eight o'clock.

speechtext:

committee proposed an amendment to this bill. Should we not know where the amendment fits in?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There are some amendments.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 to' 6 inclusive agreed to.
On section 7-Powers of the company.

If hon.
members will read the powers of the company they will at once be impressed with the far-reaching powers that are sought. I only desire to call attention to this phase of it. The real object of the company, I assume, is to incorporate an air transportation line or lines. But this company can carry on the business of bus proprietors, and builders and manufacturers. It can also carry on the business of insurance. I should like to have some assurance that the superintendent of insurance is cognizant of

Fundy Air Lines

the provisions of this bill. Would the promoter be good enough to tell the committee if this bill has the imprimatur of the superintendent of insurance? I wish to point out to this committee that the powers here are almost unheard of. I am not going to vote against the principle of the bill. I want to see the proprietors, the incorporators, get a charter to incorporate an aeroplane company, but I do not want them to go into the business of insurance; I do not think they ought to go into the business of a bus company, and above everything else I do not think they ought to go into the business of stock jobbing, because that is in this bill too. I am surprised to find that they are asking for so many powers. I wonder whether the committee gave consideration to all the powers sought and what reasons were assigned by the promoters for asking for the multiplicity of powers. I suggest that this is a kind of blanket affair. They want a great deal more than they ought to receive from this House of Commons. I merely point that out to the committee and to the Minister of Transport who is in his place at this time. I wonder whether he has taken cognizance of the tremendous powers asked for by this company. They have almost enough power to hang a man. I wonder whether his department has given consideration to that aspect of the bill and whether those considerations were in any degree considered by the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. In a nutshell, I think the pow'ers asked for are too w'ide.
I am anxious to see this company have a bill passed that will enable them to operate aeroplane transportation, because this is private enterprise which I like to see encouraged in this country, and in which many of us still believe. I am sure the minister believes in it, too, if he would only allow himself to give self-expression.
I should like the promoter to explain the omnibus powers that are asked for in this bill.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury has asked for an explanation on the three objects of this bill. His first question has to do with paragraph (f) with regard to insurance.
No; the first objection I had, if it can be called an objection, was to the power to carry on the business of omnibus proprietors and builders- paragraph (d) of section 7.
I take it, that that paragraph means they are asking for power to carry on that business in connection with air lines.
No, that is not it.
I am afraid the courts would not so interpret it.

That is the intention here. They wish power to carry on any business that would be connected with the carrying on of a successful air line. That is what they are asking here. That is what I take that paragraph to mean.
In so far as paragraph (f) is concerned, the insurance mentioned there is insurance of a kind connected with the operation which they are entitled to carry on; that is, to-

and all other kinds of insurance in connection with the operations which the company is entitled to carry on or in connection with similar operations carried on by other companies, firms or persons.
I take that to be insurance connected with the business of air lines?

That is a
fair interpretation.
I think the next objection of the hon. member for York-Sunbury was to stock jobbing. I do not think there is any power under paragraph (f) to do any stock jobbing. I take that to be paragraph (j).
There is no limit in the section to what they can do.
I do not think the company has the power implied by the hon. member for York-Sunbury.

I submit that paragraph (d) of section 7 is an alternative power to paragraphs (a), (b) and (c), and under any proper statutory interpretation is in no way connected with the business of aeroplane passage. That is not so true with respect to paragraph (f) of section 7. That paragraph expressly provides that in connection with the business of the company, the company may act as agent. Of course I think that is an appurtenance of the business of carrying on an aeroplane company and I would not have so much objection to that.
That is the omnibus business too.

But in connection with paragraphs (h), (i) and (j), I suggest these are pretty large powers. I never saw them given to a joint stock company in just this language, and I doubt if they can get it under the Companies Act of Canada or of any of the other provinces. It seems to me that the draftsman who prepared this bill must have had something in his mind when

Fundy Air Lines
he asked for all these rather extraordinary powers to deal with the distribution and capitalization among the shareholders of undivided profits and the reserves by assigning shares to the shareholders holding shares pro rata and so forth. That part could obviously be under the Joint Stock Companies Act, but certainly I do not think this company needs to have a bus franchise and to be a bus company because the same people now have a bus company that almost covers the province of New Brunswick. S.M.T. Limited is controlled by the same interests.
These are the main objections I would have and perhaps the only ones. The borrowing powers in section 8 and the ancillary and incidental powers in section 9, I have no objection to at all. If the committee desires to pass this bill as it is I am satisfied, but I think I should point these things out to the committee.

I do not think the hon. member who is sponsoring this bill has made out a very good case in respect of section 7. I should like to ask the hon. member if in the committee stage of the bill the powers to be conferred on this company by this legislation as contained in paragraph (d) namely, to carry on the business of omnibus proprietors and builders, -were discussed, and, if so, what decision was arrived at and what were the reasons given by the committee for arriving at that decision. As pointed out by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, and very properly so, the powers asked for in paragraphs (a), (b), (c) and (d) are powers that are in no way limited to the ordinary aeroplane business. I take it that is the case in so far as paragraph (e) is concerned. It says: "for the better carrying on of the business of the company". Then there are several paragraphs which are limited and perhaps confined and restricted because they come within the business of the company, but so far as paragraph (d) is concerned that is in an entirely different category. If paragraph (d) passes and it means anything, it means that we are conferring upon this company the right to carry on the business of omnibus transportation, and I think the point should be further explained.

It would be incidental to their business, I should say, to operate a bus from the airport to some central point, and it seems a fair power to ask that they be able to operate a bus to carry passengers from an aerodrome to some central point in a town or city. As far as I know there is no intention of going beyond that.

If that were done under paragraph (e) I do not think there would be

any real objection, because then it would be within the confines of the comapny's own business.
If that is the only objection of the leader of the opposition I would not mind if he moved an amendment making this a subparagraph under (e).
Would the hon. member tell us if those powers were discussed in the railway committee?
Yes.
Was there any discussion with respect to (d), and what was the explanation of the promoter or his agents?

There was no particular discussion of paragraph (d) before the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. There was a general discussion of the powers asked for in the bill, and the agents of the incorporators, who were there, offered to answer any question; but there was no particular discussion of (d).

Was the bill read to the committee, or was it just called section by section? This paragraph (d) is not limited to bus transportation within the business of the company. This is a federal charter and it gives them the right to operate omnibus service anywhere in Canada. You can get that right under provincial companies acts, and you cannot run on the highways without a licence from the provincial government, but this gives the company the right to operate interprovincial bus traffic. Did it ever occur to the committee to investigate that point and ask why this power should be requested?
This is merely incidental, I may tell my hon. friend.

If my hon. friend will pardon me, I suggest that on a proper construction of this section 7, paragraphs (a), (b), (c) and (d) are distinctly operating powers. They may be nothing but omnibus proprietors and builders which, under provincial jurisdiction, carries with it the right to use the highways. However, I am not going to say anything more about it; if the house is willing to put through legislation of this kind I am satisfied.

Just to shorten the discussion, may I say that this bill does not give the company the right to operate anything. It is an application to incorporate a company. Ordinarily applications for the incorporation of companies are granted freely by the govern-
Fundy Air Lines

ment, provided that they comply with the dominion Companies Act. I believe I am responsible for recommending to the government that in connection with companies seeking incorporation to operate air lines the approval of this House of Commons should be obtained. I did so for one reason. A year or eighteen months ago, at a time when it was impossible to operate any air line company owing to the fact that no equipment could be obtained and no gasoline could be allowed, the Secretary of State was being flooded with applications for the incorporation of companies to operate air lines, with titles that were most comprehensive. One that I recall was the Canada-West Indies Air Line company; another was the Canada-North Atlantic Air Line company, and I could name several more. At that time the government had not announced its policy dealing with the operation of air services. It was quite obvious, or at least it seemed to me quite possible, that those desiring the incorporation of companies with names such as I have mentioned intended to trade on the name of the company as an asset, which seemed to me quite improper. Therefore I asked council to require that the approval of this house be obtained in connection with the incorporation of any air line company. My thought was that those desiring incorporation should come before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines and explain why they wanted to incorporate a company, and give hon. members any explanations that might be required. I would point out that, had the government not taken that step, this company could have gone to the Secretary of State and been incorporated with any powers the incorporators wished to include in the bill.
Only those coming within the statute.

Yes, within the statute. I may add, however, that under the declared pqlicy of the government it will be quite impossible for this company to operate an air line and also a bus line. That is expressly prohibited by legislation which has been placed on the order paper; and unless the incorporators can satisfy the government that they intend to operate within declared government policy, they will not be assigned a route over which they may operate. I should like to make it clear that this bill gives the company no permission to operate anything.
I take issue with that statement. It is quite true that the bill in itself will not entitle this company to operate aeroplane transportation.
Nor bus lines.

Well,
would the minister produce any order in council that prevents the incorporation of a company to operate interprovincial bus lines? 1 assure him it is a fact that under provincial legislation a bus company may be incorporated to operate bus lines within a province. It is true in my province, and I assume it is true in all the other provinces. That may not and probably does not mean that they can operate interprovincial traffic, because when they go beyond the confines of one province according to my view of the law they come within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament ; that is to say, with respect to transportation between the provinces. I am asking the minister now if there is an order in council passed under the provisions of the War Measures Act, which prevents a company from getting a federal charter under the Companies Act, without coming to parliament. Has an order in council been passed of the same nature as that relating to aeroplane companies? I am just asking that for information. The minister shakes his head; I take it for granted that such an order in council has not been passed.

If a company wished to get a federal charter to operate bus lines, I suppose it could do so without coming to parliament, but if the company wanted to operate in more than one province it would have to satisfy each province, and also obtain operating rights from each province, in which case it would hardly need dominion incorporation to operate across provincial boundaries.

Well, they would be under the jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners with regard to rates and that sort of thing. It is quite true that you cannot operate on the highways of a province without a licence from the government of that province, even if you have a dominion charter. So that when the minister made the sweeping statement he did make, that this company could not operate anything, I think on reflection he will agree that that was just a little too large an order. I agree with him, entirely, that as the law now stands this company could not operate air lines transportation, without much more. However, I am not going into that.
Nor do I wish to be misunderstood. I am anxious that this company should have a charter to operate aeroplanes. They can then fight their way through to a satisfactory conclusion. But I think the powers they have asked for are too wide. They can do almost anything, and I am rather astonished that hon.

Fundy Air Lines
members in this house, who have legal minds, have not been aroused. Just read over the powers as to how they can switch these shares, or reserves, or undivided profits. I thought those days were pretty well over in Canada;
I imagine they would meet with a good deal of trouble from the income tax division.
However, I am not going to hold up the bill, nor did I ever intend to. But I really am astonished at the magnitude of the powers asked for to operate an aeroplane transportation company, and I think my duty is done in pointing out these facts to parliament.

speechtext: The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) said a moment ago that, if passed, this bill would give the company no power to operate anything.
