He wishes to incorporate a company; that is all.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It seems to me that if the incorporation of the company is granted by the bill, and the company starts in to sell shares and get itself organized, it will be in a position to do things contrary to the policies laid down by the minister when he spoke on March 17. I refer in particular to what he said on that date. He said that one reason for halting expansion was that the young men who should have a prominent part in any such expansion are overseas on combat duty.
What about these men; they were all overseas?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
On the other hand the minister pointed out it was not too early to plan for orderly and rapid expansion of our domestic aviation. I wholly agree with the two statements the minister made on that occasion. I am wondering whether the incorporation of this company does not give them
certain powers, and give them the right to get started, to sell their shares, and actually vitiate the two principles the minister laid down. I particularly emphasize the minister's suggestion that the expansion of our air services should be on an orderly basis.
I do not agree with the hon. member for York-Sunbury, that the way to achieve orderly expansion is to go on giving wide-open privileges to private enterprise. It seems to me that, to be consistent with the position he took on March 17, the Minister of Munitions and Supply should oppose the passing of this bill.

I was going to remark that in view of the fact that the house has not yet hadi an opportunity of considering legislation of a similar class to be brought down by the minister, namely, that of setting up a transport board for aviation, and other legislation pertinent to the working out of the government's policy, it is premature to ask hon. members to support this measure. I would favour withholding support of the bill until such time as government legislation in the field of aviation has come before the house, and until we have had an opportunity of understanding it.

In justice to the promoters of the bill, I would say that the five names mentioned in section 1 meet 1.00 per cent the suggestion made that returned men are to be given opportunities to operate aeroplane companies-men returned from the last war. I know all these men, with one exception. Mr. Rogers has to his credit in the last war the destruction of eleven German aircraft. Mr. Ritchie was a gallant soldier in the last war, and up to a recent date rendered yeoman service in this war in organizing the army in militarj^ district No. 7. Mr. Bell is a personal friend of mine; and he, too, had a most creditable war record. Mr. Kenneth C. Irving, who will be head of the company, also had a fine record in the last war. I do not know Mr. Hodgins personally, but I am informed that he, too, is a veteran of the last war. So that these men qualify 100 per cent for the minister's definition1-although I do not suppose the minister thinks that anyone who is a non-soldier should not be allowed to be engaged in the aeroplane business.
I say this in justice to these men. I am anxious to see the bill go through, but I submit that the powers they have asked for are really beyond reason, for an aeroplane transportation company.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
Export permit branch, administration, $153,805.

When the committee took recess at six o'clock the minister was about to give some information with respect to the number of export permits that had been refused and why they were refused. While he is giving us that information, perhaps he could also tell us who comprise this shipping board.
We are dealing with the export permit branch, not the shipping board.
The minister was going to give us information with respect to the permits that had been refused.
We have not in Ottawa the number of export permits that have been refused. I can get that information and give it later to the hon. member or submit it in any other way.

Where does the branch operate?
3340	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Trade and Commerce
In Ottawa. I made a mistake in using the words "in Ottawa".
How many export permits have been issued for grain from the western provinces to the United States direct, not through lake shippers?
No permits are required for the export of No. 1, 2 or 3 northern wheat, and those are the grades that are being exported.
What about feed wheat?

The export of feed wheat requires a permit.
Mr.' PERLEY: How many were issued?
I have not that information here, but possibly I can get it.
How many commodities require export permits, and what are they?
Practically everything.
That is what I thought. Has anything been overlooked? A man cannot even export his wife.
In connection with what countries are export permits required?
All countries with which we do business.
That is a most illuminating answer.
It is comprehensive.

It is
intended to conceal. Name the countries.

If I understand the hon. member correctly, he is asking about shipments to other countries, and he wants me to name the countries with which we do business and in connection with which export permits are required. I said, all countries with which we do business. That is a comprehensive answer. I cannot give any other answer unless I itemize them. I could start in with the countries on this hemisphere, then take the United Kingdom, Australia- and various other countries of the world.
That is the answer; the American countries and certain others. That is a reasonable request.
The figure referred to by the hon. member covers export permits that were refused during the year ending March, 1943.
That is the last report we have.
Those are the figures to which the hon. member is now referring. I have not the figures as to the number of export permits refused for the year ending March 31, 1944.
The minister stated this afternoon that 99,153 applications for export permits had been granted, and I was wondering why he could not give us the number that had been refused.

I have not that information here. My hon. friend wanted to know the personnel of the export control committee. They are as follows: Mr. Mallory, of the Department of Trade and Commerce, is chairman of the committee, and the other members are Mr. Adams, of the foreign exchange control board, Mr. English of the Department of Trade and Commerce, Mr. Angus, of the Department of External Affairs, Mr. Geddes of the wartime prices and trade board, Mr. Taylor and Mr. Sproule of the wartime industries control board.
The committee must have been enlarged considerably since 1943, because the last report shows the salaries and that there were not nearly as many employed in 1943.
There are no salaries paid to the members of the committee.

They are
all civil servants?
Yes.
What salaries will be paid out of this vote?
We are asking for $105,420 for 1944-45 salaries.
That is a considerable increase over last year.

An increase of $6,270.

War Appropriation-Trade and Commerce
The last report of the auditor general shows $65,907 for salaries.
I believe that is two years old.

That is just another evidence of how difficult it is to get information with respect to the minister's department. I have here, for instance, a report on the grain business in Canada, dealing with the 1942 crop. That is two years old. We are approaching the 1943-44 crop, but we have no report more recent than this one which is two years old. The minister now says that the auditor general's report is two years old in giving the salaries. How can we make comparisons if we do not know what was paid for salaries last yeai ?
The salaries paid last year amounted to $99,150, and we are asking for an increase this year of $6,270.

What is the basis or what are the bases upon which export permits are granted or refused? What is the policy and who decides the policy? Does this export permit board decide it, or is it a matter of government policy in a given case or with respect to a given commodity?

I gave that information this afternoon. It considers applications for export permits and refuses or grants after consultation with the various administrators and controllers. Members of the committee will understand that we are the machinery through which these export permits are handled. Representations are made to us by other departments of government and by controllers and administrators, and the applications are then refused or approved.

Then it is
not purely an administrative body but a body with judicial functions. But it is not an entirely independent body. Its deliberations and its decisions are based upon the representations that may be made to it not only by applicants for export permits but by the controllers and what not set up by the government. I have in mind the export of seed potatoes within a few weeks. Some of these boards are given pretty wide powers. Do they ever consult the minister in a given case?
Oh, yes.
In all cases?
Not in all cases.

In how
many?
It would be a fairly limited number.
So that the control of the export trade of this country through the issue of export permits is in the hands of a group of civil servants and the government has ceased to function as such.
Oh, no.

That is
what it comes to. They have fairly wide powers. I know of one particular case where seed potatoes were required very badly by our neighbours to the south. We were anxious to get in there in peace time. We would have given anything to establish a trade with the southern states in our seed potatoes from New Brunswick. But there was always considerable difficulty in getting a permit. I must say that in the case I had in point for one of my colleagues the board were very decent indeed when the facts were placed before them, and the permit was issued. But that is not always the case. Very wide powers are being given to these boards, and I am just wondering whether it is wise for the country to vest such wide powers in a group of civil servants, who, after all, are not business men. Not one of them could be called a business man.

The export permit board does not take it upon itself to decide these matters without being guided largely by the administrators and controllers and, in the case of food products, by the advice of the Department of Agriculture. As I said before, the board is largely the administrative machinery.

The board
then can of its own powers grant or refuse a permit, notwithstanding the representations that may be made against such a course by some of these controllers or administrators?
That would be possible.
I imagine the regulations are wide enough and extensive enough for that.

I
would say so.

Here is a board that is exercising judicial functions, and there is discretion in the board. As I under-

3342	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Trade and Commerce
stand the minister, the board is not entirely bound by the representations that may be made either by the applicant or by others concerned. So that it must be exercising a judicial discretion and can of its own motion overrule the representations made to it. Is that a fact?
It can, but almost invariably it follows the advice given to it by the administrators.

Has there been any increase in the number of permits granted over last year and over the year before that? What are the figures for last year and the year before? How long does it take to have an export permit issued after it has been applied for?
It depends entirely on the commodity. Some can be granted in a matter of hours. Some may take a day or two or a little longer.
How many applications were refused in the last fiscal year and what were the commodities? I think the (minister ought to have that information here.
I shall be glad to get that information.

The minister did not answer my question. How many permits were issued last year and the year before and was there an increase over the year previous? Is it the policy at the present time to increase as much as possible the number of export permits granted, in order to increase our external trade?

I have not the exact figures, but there has been a substantial increase in the number of permits granted this year over last year. We are guided to a very large extent by the administrator. One reason why the board operates under the Department of Trade and Commerce is that the department is necessarily anxious to promote trade and business in every way and our approach to the matter of granting export permits is a sympathetic one.
Does the minister feel that everything possible is being done to grant these permits?
Yes.

Is it the policy of the department to increase trade, and does the minister review from time to time the refusals to grant permits so as to see how matters line up? What responsibility does he take for refusal of permits?

Any refusal is referred to the board for review.
!
That does not come to me except in the odd case. A question was asked about the actual number of permits issued in 1942-43 and 1943-44. They are respectively: 87,400 and 99,153.

I desire to praise the minister for having said not long ago that we shall need a large number of ships for our trade after the war. Canada is an exporting nation and we shall have to find ships to convey our goods to all countries of the world. We shall need aeroplanes also and all other means of transport, and I hope there will be true collaboration and cooperation between the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Transport in order that our trade may be the largest after the war and, if possible, before the end of the war. The minister has men who are well trained in several commercial observation posts in all the countries that are not occupied by the enemy. But may I tell him this-and I want him to listen closely to what I tell him now, and not be disturbed by anyone while I am addressing the Chair on a matter like this. I say that we should have commercial independence in Canada. I am not for the political independence of Canada now.
Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury: Not yet.

I will ask the hon. member for York-Sunbury not to try to be a mind-reader, because we shall put a fez on his head if he does-and something else. We have to be commercially independent, and if we go to South America as little brothers of big Uncle Sam we shall not be as well received as if we went there as Canadians, as citizens of a great and proud country. If we are under the tutelage of British ambassadors, ministers and consuls; if our commercial agents are not independent of them, in order to compete with them in trade, then our export trade will be a fiasco. I should like every serious-minded business man in the country to hear what is said now. If they want progress intrade; if they want to be successful in implanting their trade in other countries, next to British trade agents or Chinese trade agents or African trade agents, or any others, they must be entirely free. I thought it was a-great mistake when the Prime Minister announced the appointment of a Canadian consul general in New York and when he said that this official would work in cooperation with the British embassy. That was all wrong. Why? Because -the duty of the Minister of Trade and Commerce is to see to it that all Canadian traders compete with the traders of any other nation of the world. I want the

War Appropriation-Trade and Commerce
minister to Temember this because I speak to him as friend to friend and I know that he means well-
Beware of the Greeks.

-and I know he is an able minister, a much abler minister than the last one in the Bennett cabinet. I say that with full knowledge and I appreciate the applause of the committee as I say that. It is true.
I do not say the other one meant badly, but I say that the minister we have now is much more competent than the one that was in charge at that time, and this I say because his predecessor, who may be illustrious in other ways, had no broad vision of trade such as the present one has. That is why I think it is so important that, instead of restrictions being applied by the export permit board or any other board, every facility should be given to red-blooded Canadians to export to other countries all the goods that are not required in this country for consumption. They must rely on the constant assistance of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and then it will not be for us to go after any other country for trade protection. We have ships. We have a fine merchant marine. We have been told that our navy has expanded considerably for the protection of our trade routes, and we shall have powerful rivals. I would ask hon. gentlemen to keep the peace for a moment. If they want to chatter, they should not sing a hymn too loudly.
I will say another thing to the minister. Not so long ago I read in the press that at the conclusion of the war or perhaps at the end of this year the merchant marine of the United States will comprise fifty thousand vessels and will be as large as all the combined merchant marines of the world. It is possible for Canadian shippers to ship their produce and goods on foreign vessels or on vessels of other countries, but it is also important that Canadian vessels be registered in Canada instead of in some other country. It is colonial to register Canadian ships in London, New York or anywhere else. It means that the owners of those ships are not sure enough of themselves to take advantage of our legislation to give credit to Canada for the vessels that are owned in Canada. I hope that the minister will not forget those observations too quickly; that he will remember them, and that since he has not the same turn of mind he will not give false interpretations to what I said as [DOT] his illustrious predecessors did in other ways.
I should like to say a few words with regard to one other matter. This matter is not of the same importance as general trade trends and
conditions. It is very difficult to get information about export permits for charcoal. There is a way of shipping charcoal in the United States and I am told that charcoal absorbs water. It is known by the exporters that some water is poured on charcoal to make it heavier and they receive a better weight. That is just as ingenious as the plans of the great Archimedes. It is apparent they must have studied physics, but they are not honest with the consignee. I will not give names below, but I shall give them later to the minister, and I shall ask him to make an investigation in due course so that the patrons of those shippers will not be deceived as to the weight of the shipment. I thank the committee for listening so generously to the few remarks which I have made, and which I made in order to promote Canadian trade and to try to relieve us of all inferiority complexes in matters that are so vital to the future of this country.

I wish to make one brief remark with respect to the export permit branch which was set up in 1941. Paragraph 2 on page 5 of the deputy minister's report is rather difficult to follow. We are told in that paragraph that 95,000 applications were received. Of those 95,000, 3,150 were refused. That would bring the total down to 91,850; yet we are told that only 87,400 permits were issued. I should like to know what happened to the 4,450. We are told that of that 87,450, 75,488 carry a $2 licence fee. Seventy-five thousand permits at $2 is $150,000; yet we are told a net revenue of $140,000 was produced. I think the minister should give an explanation of that particular paragraph, because it is not clear and may leave a wrong impression in the mind of the layman. It leaves a difficult impression in my own mind at the present time as to what it actually does mean.

In answer to the hon. member for Camrose I would point out that out of 95,000 applications for export permits, 3,150 were refused on the advice of the administrators or controllers because of the supply situation in Canada; but in addition to that a substantial number were refused by the export board itself, for purposes of economic warfare.
Who refused the 3,150?
They were refused on the advice of the administrators or controllers.

Therefore in reality, instead of only 3,150 applications being refused, 7,600 were refused.
3344	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Trade and Commerce

Yes; the remainder were refused for other reasons: For example, people on the black list or supplies for countries like Spain and Portugal where there might be a danger of the goods reaching undesirable destinations
What permits could be refused by the administrator or controller? Who had the power to cancel such permits? Is that entirely in the hands of the minister himself?

The refusal of those permits on the grounds of economic warfare is in the hands of the export board itself.
The hon. member pointed to the seeming discrepancy in the fees. The amount shown simply by multiplying the number of permits granted by the $2 fee does not take into account the rebates that were made later.

Would the minister
snlarge on that?
Then permits under $100 do not require a $2 fee.
How many were there for goods under $100 that would not carry the $2 fee?
There would be a large number. We have not the figures at the moment, but they would be substantial.
Might I have those figures?
Yes; I shall be glad to get them for the hon. member.

When may we have an opportunity to discuss the board recently set up under the direction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce by order in council P.C. 70 of January 31 last, known as the Canadian export board? Evidently there is no vote here covering the operations of this board; yet according to the Commercial Intelligence Journal for February 12, for the purposes of this board it will be provided with a revolving credit, adjustable as experience demands, to provide adequate working capital. Shall we have an opportunity of discussing the establishment of this board, its operation and the amount of capital that has been set aside for it for the next twelve months, and when may we have that opportunity?

It might be well for me to make a short state-
[Mr. Marshall.1
ment in that connection at this time. There is no vote under discussion covering this particular item. This board was not set up until January 31, 1944, and it was therefore too late to be included in the printed estimates. While there is no item under discussion, I am pleased to be able to tell hon. members of the committee some of the purposes of the board.
A number of overseas governments, for a variety of reasons, have insisted that imports into their countries must be effected by government agencies, and that import permits will not be issued for certain classes of goods. Procurement agencies have been set up in Ottawa by several governments, while others have their procurement agencies in the United States. The procurement of war supplies has been and continues to be done by the Department of Munitions and Supply. In the case of goods which are not strictly for use by the armed forces, however, it was felt that some other agency should be responsible for procurement. Even under this condition it was only after careful investigation had shown that orders were being placed elsewhere than in Canada that the Canadian export board was established by order in council P.C. 70, of January 31, 1944.
This board is acting as procurement agency for civilian goods for those countries which will not permit normal channels of trade to be used. Without the board, orders would be placed in other countries and Canada would lose valuable trade connections which would be difficult to regain for the post-war period. The export board also acts as one of the procurement agencies for the mutual aid board, handling goods which, although war supplies, are not actually munitions of war. There is, of course, close coordination between the export board and the Department of Munitions and Supply.
The export board operates on a non-profit basis and really functions as agent for overseas governments. Goods are furnished to other countries at the purchase price plus any additional charges which are necessarily incurred in completing the export transactions. The board is not competing with private enterprise and, in fact, is trying to divert business back to trade channels as and when conditions permit. When a request is received by the board from an overseas government, or from the mutual aid board administration, quotations are invited from all Canadian firms in a position to supply, or in accordance with any allocation which may have been established by the appropriate controller or administrator; thus normal trade channels and methods are utilized so far as possible.

Supply-Legislation-The Senate

One of the powers given to this board is to buy, sell, negotiate the purchase or sale of and engage in export trade in such commodities to such extent as the board may consider advisable. Does that mean the board can go into any part of Canada and buy these commodities, and then act as a sort of agent for the various companies in the sale of the commodities? For example, what work does it do in connection with agricultural products, let us say?

This board will not buy until it is actually in possession of a buying order from some other government. Then it goes out and purchases the goods for delivery to the other government. Practically it acts as an agent for the other government.

Then would the minister inform the committee how he deals with shipments for export under the mutual aid arrangement and, for instance, shipments of grain to Greece. Do the exporters require permits under the mutual aid arrangement, or does the government itself handle such shipments through some agency?
Under mutual aid they do not require export permits. In connection with shipments of wheat to Greece export permits are required.
Would the exporters secure that wheat from the wheat board and then get a permit to ship it; and would there be any commissions or brokerage fees charged on the grain?
I can answer that question now, or it can be dealt with later in connection with the export of wheat to Greece.
We might as well have it now; it will save us the necessity of asking the question again.
The wheat for export is furnished by the wheat board.
The exporters will have to get a permit from this board?
Yes, for that purpose.
Item agreed to.

I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again this day.
Progress reported.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Rradette in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The official report of iebates shows that during the previous sitting of the committee to-day the hon. member for Temiscouata used the following words in speaking about the senate:
_ They have completely lost any sense of shame in the senate, and with the exception of two or three senators for whom I have the deepest admiration, I concur in what was said by the leader of the C.C.F. party as to the abolition of that body. . . .
If they were willing to work, if they had enough initiative, they could help us, they could play the part that was allotted to them under our constitution. . . .
The senate is a nonentity in parliament at the present time just on account of the unwillingness of the senators to do something while they are sitting there. . . .
But they are like an anachronism . . . it is the realm of rolling chairs and railroading bills. . . .
, I would not be for the abolition of the senate if the senators were really up to the standard of days gone by. . . .
Another is a gentleman who had fat contracts from the Department of Munitions and Supply for being the agent of Mr. MacMillan in the province of Quebec.
The hon. gentleman was asked to withdraw these offensive statements which are prohibited under standing order 41. He refused to give a full and unqualified explanation which can be considered as satisfactory or in keeping with the dignity of the house and the mutual respect that should exist between the Senate and the House of Commons. I must insist on an unqualified withdrawal.

Mr. Chairman, will you kindly let me see the quotations? In the first place, I may tell you that I have gone to the Hansard room and I have asked them not to change an iota of their notes, an iota in the transcription of their notes, which means that I did not want to interfere with the report of Hansard, but which is not an acceptation of the transcription of the notes of Hansard in full.
For instance, in the first quotation I am reported as having said, "They have completely lost any sense of shame in the senate." I never said that. I said, "They have completely lost any usefulness in the senate." And I said

And with the exception of two or three senators for whom I have the deepest admiration I concur in what was said by the leader of the C.C.F. party as to the abolition of that body.
That was said-the second part.
Supply-Legislation-The Senate

Bult, at page 3329, I am quoted as having said:
I would not infringe the rule 'by saying that the senate is useless.
This I said. And it is naturally connected to the first part of the sentence; and I hoped that it would have been in the mind of the touchy little Emily Post-and when I use that expression I do not mean the Chair at all. Then it goes on:
If they were willing to work; if they had enough initiative, they could help us; they could play the part that was allotted to them under our constitution.
In order to show my willingness to cooperate, I am ready to withdraw, "If they were willing to work"-that phrase-and the sentence would read:
If they had enough initiative they could help us; they could play the part that was allotted to them under our constitution.
I do not think that sentence, as corrected, is against the standing order that you quoted.
There is another sentence:
The senate is a nonentity in our parliament at the present time, just on account of the unwillingness of the senators to do something while they are sitting there.
This I have withdrawn, and I do not see why any member should be obliged to withdraw the same thing twice. I remember that on a previous occasion, when Mr. Bennett was Prime Minister, he forced me-he tried to force me to withdraw a second time a thing I already had withdrawn, for the sake of peace, and to show my spirit of cooperation, and what the Prime Minister calls good will. But I do not see why the torture should be imposed upon a member of parliament who says a thing like that, and who has to kneel down twice. I am sure, and I believe in your fairness you will agree that a statement withdrawn once must be settled forever, until it is repeated again. But when I had to do so it was in explaining a case. And it is not because I have read the record that I shall be forced a second time to withdraw.
Then:
But they are like an anachronism.
This was declared in order-or not out of order. Therefore I have nothing to withdraw here. Then:
It is the realm of rolling chairs and railroading bills.
I made a mistake here, and I confess it. After having seen the performance on divorce bills, it is not the Senate that is the realm of rolling chairs and railroading bills; it is the House of Commons. We passed I do not know how many bills in eight or ten minutes, but

I was the only member to make any protest against them, although in many other instances other members have protested against them. But if we did not railroad bills to-night, then bills were never railroaded in parliament. Five pages of bills in five minutes-a page a minute; think of that! And in the senate they pass our bills over there, just the same as we pass their bills here. They are doing it just as fast. It is not railroading; it is the airways; it is the T.C.A., at 200 miles an hour.
"Of rolling chairs"-I withdraw it.
Then:
I would not 'be for the abolition of the senate if the senators were really up to the standard of days gone by.
I will substitute for it:
I would not be for the abolition of the senate if all the senators were really up to the standard of days gone by.
Then:
Another is a gentleman who had fat contracts from the Department of Munitions and Supply for being the agent of Mr. Macmillan in the province of Quebec.
Perhaps I did not express myself clearly enough. I did not have in mind any offensive remark against that gentleman personally. What I meant was that he was agent of Mr. Macmillan, and while he was agent of Mr. Macmillan he had huge contracts from the Department of Munitions and Supply. Afterwards I spoke of reward. By "reward" I meant a senatorship; and I would have said it if I had not been interrupted by the Minister of National Defence. I could not finish.
Further, I had something very fine to say about the fourth last appointee from the province of Quebec, Senator Lesage, who deserved an appointment to the senate, because he had been political organizer for the Liberal party for twenty-five years. And a man who had done that job for a quarter of a century deserves recognition. But I did not have an opportunity to say it. My remarks were cut right in the middle by someone who was exceedingly touchy. And it cannot be an insult to a man to say to him that he had big contracts from the department. And, mark you, there is something that is more important: I used the present tense in that case. I said:
One is a gentleman who has a fat salary.
This is present; it is not past.
Another is a gentleman who had-
And . this is the record of Hansard-
-fat contracts from the Department of Munitions and Supply for being the agent of Mr. Macmillan in the province of Quebec. The third had no political background whatever.

Supply-Legislation-The Senate
I wish to relieve from your mind the idea that I thought of imputing any bad motive to Macmillan's agent, when I spoke of that. What I had in mind was that he had enough in having a big contract, and that there was no reason to appoint him to the senate to give him that reward, or anything. I did not use "award"; I used "reward". And I would have said, "For reward, a senatorship", if I had not been interrupted like that by the Minister of National Defence. I appreciate the compliment when he said that I knew the rules quite well. I do not pretend to be that good; that is an exaggeration.
To conclude I want to tell you, Mr. Chairman, that I abide by the rules; I abide by your decision, but at the same time I want to defend the rights of members of parliament. This is not a pink tearoom; this is the place where we have the right to discuss the business of the nation. I contend that if there is an item in the estimates which permits a discussion of everything that pertains to the senate, it is item 112 of the main estimates. I tell you that we live in a false atmosphere. I wonder if it is like that around the table at Barclay's bank. I have never been there and I shall never be there. We must talk like men, men who have a tremendous responsibility. This responsibility rests not only on the minister; the members of parliament have a responsibility as great if not greater, because they are the immediate representatives of the people. During the campaign through the west in 1941 the Prime Minister regretted that he had no direct contact with the people. We have.
When I speak here as a member of parliament there are things that I have the right to say, and I deny to any minister the right to interrupt me on a point of order and saying that I should not rise in my place. I have not the time to write my speeches because I have a voluminous correspondence to attend to. I speak extemporaneously; I do not speak for the students and I do not expect that my speeches will be translated two thousand years hence. I speak for to-day; I speak on the problems of to-day and I do that with tremendous emphasis.
I am not going to be bullied by any one of my colleagues with calls to the Chair when I have the right to speak, when I have the right to express the views of my electors as well as my own. I protest solemnly and strongly and energetically and with the greatest vehemence against the tactics of the Minister of National Defence who would like to see members of parliament act as mummies in the House of Commons. The ideal member for him would be the member who would keep his arms folded and his big back on the chair and never rise in the house, who would always nod yes. He wants a yes-man. I am not a yes-man; I am a no-man to him; I am a no-man to any suggestion that he will make because if he makes a good one it will be wrongly presented and wrongly done. That is why I affirm my independence as a member of parliament. I cannot tolerate any more interruptions from any minister, and especially from the Minister of National Defence.

Mr. Chairman, as you might anticipate, I do not propose following the hon. member in the byways and highways which he has pursued in connection with this particular matter. I am only rising here as I did this afternoon because of my duty, happening to be at the moment leader of the house. I feel it to be my responsibility to endeavour to preserve not only the dignity of this house but the dignity of parliament which consists of the House of Commons and the Senate. The suggestion by any hon. member that he has the right to speak, that he will not be hobbled or that he will not be stopped by me or by anybody else leaves me quite cold because there is no suggestion of that kind at all. All that an hon. member needs to do in order to preserve his right to speak is to keep within the rules of the house.
I always do.

It was for the purpose of calling attention to that that I regretfully had to rise this afternoon at a time when we should have been engaged in something other than discussing matters of the kind the hon. member discussed this afternoon. He had a right to make his speech on the particular item, but at the same time I felt that the dignity of the other branch of this parliament should be preserved as we would expect the dignity of this house to be preserved if the tables were reversed and if any such remarks were made regarding the House of Commons as were made regarding the other chamber by the hon. member this afternoon.
The hon. member has gone pretty far in connection with this matter. He could not resist the opportunity to take a fling at the individual who happens at the moment to be leading the house. I shall leave that for some other time, but there are some things which the hon. member has not done and which I submit he should do. Notwithstanding the fact that he does not take suggestions from me, I venture to suggest to you, Mr. Chair-
Supply-Legislation-The Senate

man, that the well known grace of his race ought to prompt him to make a full and unreserved withdrawal of any imputations which he may have passed upon the other chamber or its members.
The first statement which was mentioned and which is recorded on the blue sheets of
Hansard the hon. member says that he did not say; that Hansard wrongly reported him. All I can say is that it is in Hansard at page 3328. Tins is the statement:
They have completely lost any sense of shame in the Senate, and with the exception of two or three senators for whom I have the deepest admiration, I concur in what was said by the leader of the C.C.F. party as to the abolition of that body.
If the hon. member had withdrawn it; if he had simply left it and stated that he had not said it, that would have been one thing. But the hon. member did not do that. What he said was that he proposed to substitute for the words "sense of shame" the word "usefulness." He thought that that would cure the difficulty, that that would make words which were exceedingly offensive, if not wholly inoffensive, at least less offensive. The definition "offensive" as given by the Oxford dictionary is this:
Offensive

1. Pertaining or tending to attack; aggressive; adapted or used for purposes of attack; characterized by attacking. Opposite to defensive. Hurtful, injurious. Giving, or of a nature to give offence; displeasing; annoying; insulting. Causing unpleasant sensations; now, nauseous, repulsive. Of the nature of a transgression. The offensive: the position or attitude of attack; aggressive action.
I suggest that you take the revision which the hon. member has made of his speech, the substitution, of "usefulness" for "sense of shame," and add to that the other statements which he has made with regard to the senate and which appear in the extracts which you have just read-such as this statement:
If they were willing to work; if they had enough initiative, they could help us; they could play the part that was allotted to them under our constitution.
Add that to the statement that they have completely lost their usefulness, and then add this statement:
The senate is a nonentity in our parliament at the present time, just on account of the unwillingness of the senators to do something while they are sitting there.
I ask you if the change from the words "sense of shame" to the word "usefulness" helps a great deal in making the language used less offensive to the other chamber. I ask hon. members to put themselves in the position, and I ask the hon. member to put himself in the position of a member of the House of Commons reading a statement of

that kind being made by a member of the other chamber with regard to this House of Commons, the tatement that this house had completely lost its usefulness, that they were not willing to work, that because of their unwillingness to do something they are a nonentity in parliament, that if they had enough initiative they could help. I ask him; I ask you, Mr. Chairman, and I ask the members of this committee if they would not consider that that was offensive. Those are the words which the hon. member has still left on the record, and added to them is the statement which he made about one member of the other chamber, with regard to which he makes a rather curious explanation. He says:
Another is a gentleman who had fat contracts from the Department of Munitions and Supply for being the agent of Mr. Macmillan in the province of Quebec.
Perhaps my mind is too suspicious; perhaps I am too touchy, but if I were reading that statement I would have thought that the gentleman there was being accused of having used his position as an agent of Mr. Macmillan, who was under the Department of Munitions and Supply first as timber controller and afterwards as director of Wartime merchant shipping for the purpose of obtaining fat contracts from the Department of Munitions and Supply.
I rise to a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman. I do not want my statement to be distorted by anyone.

I am stating, Mr. Chairman, that that is the construction any reasonable man would put upon that particular passage, and that is the thing which, it seems to me, is about as offensive as anything which could possibly be said by a member of this house with regard to a member of the other house. There is a sort of special pleading in connection with the matter, because the hon. member does make some suggestion that he thought the member of the other house having gotten contracts, would not need any more contracts in view of the fact that he had attained a position in the senate. That explanation may satisfy the hon. member for Temiscouata, but I do not think it will satisfy the public who see that particular statement on the record with regard to a member of the senate.
Once again, Mr. Chairman, the minister has not understood what I have said.

I am speaking of the exact words as they are recorded, and which the hon. member admits were recorded, with regard to that hon. gentleman.

Supply-Legislation-The Senate
The minister pays no attention to my explanation.

I submit that having done, as I think he has, a very grave injustice to the members of the other house and to a particular member of that house in that passage, I would have thought he would have unreservedly withdrawn any imputations of the kind.
Which I have done.
If the hon. member says he has done it-
Surely.
Then so far as I am concerned the incident is closed, but I understood my hon. friend to do almost everything but that.
That is most unfair and I protest, Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege.
Do I take it, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member does withdraw unqualifiedly any imputations against the senate or any members thereof?
I do not want my statements to be distorted by anyone.
I rise to a point of order.

I am on my feet, Mr. Chairman. How is it that I have to sit down when
he rises?

I am rising to a point of order. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this is a matter which is not debatable. The matter is before the Chair, and all I am saying is that if the hon. gentleman does withdraw unqualifiedly any imputations which he has made against the senate and its members, then so far as I am concerned the incident is closed. The remarks he has made about me do not disturb me in the least. But I submit that it is not a matter that we should debate.
I ask you, Mr. Chairman, if I have to withdraw twice?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
No doubt the committee realizes that it is a delicate question to settle. Several arguments have been brought up by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). An hon. member of this house has a right before the orders of the day are called or in committee to see that he is properly reported in Hansard. That is the privilege accorded to every member of parliament. The hon. member for Temiscouata has stated this evening that he did not use the word "shame" but that he used the word "useless." I feel
that the committee must accept the statement of the hon. member for Temiscouata on that point.
This afternoon I gave a ruling on the use of the word "nonentity" as applied to the senate, and the hon. member for Temiscouata withdrew that statement unequivocally as will be found in the record of Hansard for this afternoon.
The only question that is left as to which I am not absolutely satisfied in my own mind, although I listened very attentively to the hon. member for Temiscouata, is the allusion that he made this afternoon to a gentleman who was appointed to the senate, stating that he had received fat contracts. I listened very attentively to the hon. member's explanation this evening but that matter is still left on the border-line to some extent. Although I want to believe that he intended no reflection whatever on the character of the senate and of the senator that he had in mind-
Not at all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
-from the repeated
statements made by the hon. member for Temiscouata that he has just made at this sitting, I believe I am voicing the sentiments of the majority of the committee when I say that his explanation should be accepted.
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I report progress?
No.

I am only submitting this, that the statements to which I have' referred are the hon. member's statements with regard to the senate having lost any usefulness and also its unwillingness to work, which simply means that members of the senate are there not only neglecting but unwilling to do their duty.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
On that point the hon. member for Temiscouata has said this evening that he did not want to use the expression that the senate is useless.
Some 'hon. MEMBERS: Withdraw the whole statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I agree that the hon. member should withdraw it now.
I will bow to your decision, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Do I understand there is an unqualified withdrawal of all the aspersions of any kind whatsoever that have been made against the other house by the hon. member for Temiscouata?

Supply-Legislation-The Senate

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I listened very attentively to what the hon. member for Temis-couata said a few moments ago, and took notes of his statements, and I believe that that is the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: May we have the assurance that that is the case? '
How many times do I have to repeat it to deaf ministers?
Ask him the question, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will ask the question. I will ask the hon. member for Temiscouata, who, I know, wants to be fair to himself and to the committee, if he makes an unqualified withdrawal?

I cannot do more than I have done, Mr. Chairman. I have done it gradually, one by one. I am not going to bend before any minister. I respect you, Mr. Chairman, and I will abide by the Chair's decision, whatever you decide. I cannot say more than that. I do not abide by anything that is said by the Minister of National Defence.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I know the hon. member realizes that the committee wants an unqualified withdrawal.
If the majority of the committee wants it, I will give it.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is not unqualified.

If I am told to withdraw statements distorted by the Minister of National Defence, I cannot do it. I do not want to do an injustice to anyone. I observe the golden rule, and if I have offended against the rules of the house in anything I have said I have already given a satisfactory explanation which has been accepted by the Chair. After it has been accepted by the Chair, I hear roars from powerful breasts telling me to do something else.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I listened attentively to the hon. member for Temiscouata and thought it was an unqualified withdrawal, and I have rendered my decisions accordingly, but apparently the members of the committee do not feel that it was such. I will therefore ask the hon. member for Temiscouata if he makes an unqualified withdrawal.

I always abide by your rulings, Mr. Chairman, and I do so now even for those who do not have ears to hear.
fMr. Ian A. Mackenzie.]

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is not an unqualified withdrawal.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. member withdraw unqualifiedly?
I abide by your decision.
No!
That is not a withdrawal.

Well, what is this? Is it a torture room? It is most ridiculous when ministers want to humiliate a member of parliament. I will not kneel down. I bend before the Chair, but I kneel down before no one else.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must ask the hon. member for an unqualified answer, yes or no. Does he withdraw?
I abide by your decision.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

I shall have to name the hon. member, and that is one of the duties which I am loath to discharge, and which I want to use only as a last resort. I must ask the hon. member for an unqualified withdrawal.
Well, all right, sir.

subtopic: 'PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration in com-mitte of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Usley

Mr. Bradette in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall item 1 carry?

Item agreed to.
Canadian shipping board -administration, $98 300
Revolving chartering fund, $500,000.

Will the minister
explain the reason for the increase in the vote?

War Appropriation-Trade and Commerce

The amount asked for, for 1944-45, is $598,300. There is a revolving fund of $500,000. The details are: salaries, $30,000; cost of living bonus and other pay-list items, $2,700; travelling $36,000; telegrams and telephones, $15,000; printing and stationery, $2,000; miscellaneous, $2,000; allowance Washington representative, $7,000; office accommodation, Vancouver, $3,600. This increase is on account of the fact that during the forthcoming year it will be necessary for the shipping board to appoint a representative in India and a senior shipping clerk for the Great Lakes, St. Lawrence division. The revolving fund revenue far exceeds the total expenditure for the operation of this entire board.

I thought something like that had taken place in connection with the revolving fund because in 1942-43 the allotment was $350,000, of which only $15,000 was expended. Could the minister give the figures as to the actual amount
I cannot hear the hon. member.

Well, I am talking as loud as I can. I wonder if the minister would give the amount actually earned during this last year 1943-44, and the expenditures. Certainly, if there is a profit, I do not see why you need $500,000 of a revolving fund. It is said that the earnings far exceed the expenditures. If that is so, what is the object of having a revolving fund of $500,000?

The total expenditure for 1943-44 was $128,529.77, and the total revenue for the same period was $351,666.69, or, in the year's operation, a net surplus of $223,136.92. The revolving fund of $500,000 is an amount that is used for the chartering of vessels, and any earnings go to the consolidated revenue fund. Possibly we could get along with a smaller amount, but it is not considered advisable to ask for less.
Does the surplus go into the consolidated revenue fund, or is it kept in the revolving fund?
It goes back to the consolidated revenue fund.
Who are the members of the shipping board and what are their duties.

The members of the board are:	Mr. A. L. W.
MacCallum, chairman and director of shipping; Mr. F. E. Bawden, vice-chairman, who deals with the director of trade routes and steamship subsidies, and who is an official of the Depart-ment'of Trade and Commerce; Captain J. W.
Kerr, supervisor of nautical services, from the transport department; Captain Eric S. Brand, director of the trade division, naval service, Department of National Defence; Mr. T. C. Lockwood, transport controller, Department of Transport; and Mr. J. S. Macdonald, Counsel of the Department of External Affairs. This position of Mr. Macdonald's is temporarily vacant following his appointment as high commissioner to Newfoundland. Mr. A. W. Merriam represents the Department of National Revenue, and the secretary is Mr. B. A. Macdonald, Canadian government trade commissioner on loan to the forces at the present time.
What are their duties?
These men speak for each of their departments.

I am not quite clear
on the question of where this surplus goes, because in the previous year we are told that the earnings were carried forward to a special account. Would the minister explain what is meant there? If the money is all shown in the consolidated revenue fund, why does it state in the auditor general's report that those earnings are transferred into a special account?
The earnings from the ship voyages carry on from month to month, and the moneys are carried into this special fund and turned back possibly at the end of the year.

Does the harbour board
play any part in the working of the board?
No.
Are any of the members of the Montreal harbour board members of this board?
No

Does the harbour board
play any part in the export shipments permits, and so on?
No; simply a matter of close cooperation.
With the harbour board?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Shipping priorities committee - administration, $47,380.
Why the decrease?
Why the increase?^

It
is a decrease.

War Appropriation-Trade and Commerce
The auditor general's report is confusing.

The general decrease in estimated expenditure is rendered possible by the faot that this branch is now believed to have achieved its maximum expansion with expenses being consequently more fixed and more accurately predictable.

Item agreed to.
Gift of wheat to Greece, $8,500,000.

There is an increase of
$2,500,000 in this amount, and a very great increase over the previous year as shown in the auditor general's report. Would the minister explain that, and also is there any flour going to Greece other than wheat under -the mutual aid, or does it all go in the form of wheat?

This all goes in the form of wheat. The additional amount required is on account of the increase in -the price of wheat, together with the fact that improved shipping conditions have made it possible for -the relief commission to obtain more consistent sailings and in that way send larger ampunts.
How do you arrive at the price of this wheat? What does it cost the wheat board?
The wheat is delivered from that which the government has taken over and the price is $1.25 a bushel.

Is there any difference in
the price of this wheat so far as the wheat board is concerned and the price of the wheat shipped to other countries under mutual aid?
Not under mutual aid, no.
The same price prevails?
Yes.
Based on Fort William?
Yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to take just a moment to speak in wholehearted support of this item and the policy that makes it possible. I wish to take a. moment to read an extract or two from the April, 1944, issue of "International Affairs", a copy of which came to my desk a few days ago. Included in this publication is a report of an address given at Chatham House on November 16, 1943, by George Exintaris, who was at one time governor general of Macedonia. He escaped from Greece to Great Britain in July, 
1943. In his address Mr. Exintaris dealt with the steady deterioration of the situation in Greece following the German occupation in April, 1941. There are two or three sentences that I should like to quote, and they are as follows:
Between October 1941 and April 1942 the spectacle of Athens and Piraeus was -truly tragic. One used to see in the streets people suddenly dropping dead from exhaustion. At night the lamentations of the old and the cries of starving women and children, cries of unappeased hunger, haunted the passer-by and transformed, as it were, most of the streets of Athens into one whole wailing wall of Jerusalem. Mortality assumed terrifying proportions. In Athens and Piraeus alone in the five months from October 1941 to February 1942 the number of deaths above the normal was thirty-five -thousand.
Mr. Exintaris goes on to point out how the situation kept getting worse. Then we come to this sentence which gave me a real sense of pride when I came across it:
Between the end of 1942 and June 1943- the situation improved slightly. This was due to:
(a) the regular monthly dispatch from Canada of eighteen thousand tons (fifteen thousand tons of wheat, three thousand tons of beans and small quantities of powdered milk).
The speaker went on to give two other reasons for the slight improvement at that time, but I call attention to the fact that the first reason for the improvement to which he was referring was this regular monthly dispatch from Canada consisting mainly of our gift of wheat to these people. However, Mr. Exintaris went on to point out that the situation has even since then deteriorated and that the need is exceedingly great. He ends this part of his address by saying:
If those in whose hands these decisions are entrusted could visit Greece -for one day only and see for themselves the extent of the tragedy, they would, I -feel sure, -take steps to alleviate the sufferings of a -people whose only fault, if fault it -be, is the execution of their duty and the defence of their homes.
I think all of us in this committee should be justly proud that Canada is able to alleviate even to this slight extent the terrible suffering of the people of Greece. Let us hope that we may learn out of this experience the value of trying to help meet the needs of humanity' the world over. These are days when we are seeing many things that are terrifying, the suffering that is going on due to this conflict in which we are engaged. I take just this moment because it seems to me that it is encouraging to realize that at the same time we are learning some other things as the desirability of endeavouring to help our brother men when they are in dire need.
I rise to support wholeheartedly the policy of the Canadian people-the government will

War Appropriation-Trade and Commerce
not mind it if I put it in that way in this instance-in making this gift to the needy and heroic people of Greece.

Following the hon. member's remarks I might just mention that as of May 9 of this year Canada has sent a total of 11,172,308 bushels.
I am occasionally asked as to the certainty of this wheat, and all of this wheat, getting to the people for whom it is intended. Just recently I have had an opportunity of discussing this matter with people who are positively in touch with this, and I shall take just a moment or two to give the committee some information given to me by those people. As a direct result of wheat shipped by Canada to Greece three million Greeks are being provided with a basic bread ration of approximately two hundred grams or, roughly, half a pound a day. Greek officials have estimated that many hundreds of thousands of Greek lives have been saved by Canada's contribution. The wheat shipments have given the Greek nation the certainty of being able to secure bread freely and fairly. Though not large, the bread ration has been a vital factor in sustaining Greece during her long period of suffering.
Before the war Greece used to import one-third of her foodstuffs. She was broken and impoverished by her heroic seven months' struggle against Italy and Germany. Then came the terrible famine of 1941, to which my hon. friend has just referred, when people died in the streets of starvation, and at one stage the death rate in Athens was at least ten times normal. It was against this background of suffering that Canada's wheat shipments began in the spring of 1942, under the terms of an international agreement. We are positively assured by the best authority that all our wheat has reached the Greeek people for whom it is intended. The Swedish Red Cross and the Internation Red Cross, with the Swedish government acting in a supervisory capacity, are in charge of the Greek distribution in Greece.

I can endorse what the minister has just said. Quite a number of Greeks live in the riding of Davenport, and they are extremely fine citizens. In several cases members of a family are now holding high positions in the allied service in Europe and North Africa. Some of the young men whom I know quite well not only are participating in the fighting but rendering wonderful service as interpreters. I heartily endorse the idea of sending wheat to Greece; in fact I should like to see it sent in larger quantities. Think of it for a moment; just a few million Greeks stood up like lions against Italy, who sent many hundreds of thousands of soldiers in
an attempt to conquer that little nation, but until the Germans sent division after division to support the Italians the Greeks more than held their own. The least this great country of Canada can do is to alleviate the suffering of these people as much as possible. This is one way in which we can help our own people by buying wheat from them and relieving the surplus in Canada, and at the same time help feed these starving people. I say all honour to every effort, no matter by whom made, to relieve the sufferings of the gallant Greeks.

I am heartily in favour of this gift to Greece, and I am also heartily in favour of the provisions of TJNRRA, whose provisions I hope will be sufficiently wide in scope to take care of any situation that may arise in future. But why should this wheat not be sent to Greece under the provisions of UNRRA? Was the arrangement made before UNRRA was set up, and in that case will this wheat be made available to Greece in future under UNRRA?
The hon. member is correct in thinking that this item is dealt with separately because it started before UNRRA was organized.
And in future?
We propose to carry it on in this way. It is just as good for the Greek people as in any other way.
It seems a little odd to have an organization such as UNRRA to take care of the stricken areas, and then find gifts made outside of UNRRA. Where does UNRRA begin and where does it end?
It has been pointed out to me that UNRRA does not enter into the picture in supplying goods to a country that has been overrun, until that country is liberated.

The wheat was sent
before UNRRA was thought of.

I hope the minister is assured that the wheat we send gets to the Greek people and not to the nazis, though I suppose that is a chance we must take. I heartily endorse the idea of sending this wheat to Greece. After all, the Greeks and the people of the British empire have always stood for freedom. We can never forget the great part played by Greece in fighting a delaying action at a most important time in the history of the war, when they held the fort against great odds. They knew what would happen to them; they knew the difficulties they were

I should now like to put on Hansard the statement to which I referred. It is as follows:
Work of the National Research Council
Prior to the outbreak of war the national research council was conducting scientific research and investigation in its own laboratories. It was also fostering research throughout Canada tby means of its associate committees, by grants in aid of research, and by .providing scholarships to aid in the training of young scientists. Each associate committee superintended a limited field of investigation and its membership consisted of technical and administrative men from universities, departments of government and industry, whose experience and skill were pooled in directing .the research. Through these committees the council was in [DOT]touch with laboratory personnel and facilities throughout Canada, and it acquired fairly detailed knowledge of their potentialities.
The value of this knowledge and of the council's widespread contacts became apparent as soon as war broke out. Problems which required the work of scientists were brought to the attention of the council and were either undertaken in the council's laboratories or placed with the individual or laboratory best equipped for the work. Some of the associate committees were already working in fields which merely had to be broadened in order to meet the new needs. For example, the committee on medical research, which had originally been organized to coordinate medical research for civilian needs in Canada, became the nucleus for the study of medical problems presented by the new and changed conditions of warfare on land and sea, and in the air. Similarly the Canadian committee on food preservation turned its attention from strictly peace-time food technology to studies of the means of maintaining the quality of the foodstuffs delivered to our armed forces and to the people of Great Britain. Both committees have produced sound work which will continue to be of value after hostilities cease.
Supervisors of research under certain committees whose work was of a peace-time importance only were directed to use their grants in the pursuit of specific war problems which their special training enables them to undertake. In addition, individual scientists who had been receiving grants in aid of research directly from the council also undertook war research

War Appropriation-
-Trade and Commerce
problems. All this resulted in the utilization of facilities from one end of Canada to the other in a systematic attempt to cover the tasks at hand with economy of staff and equipment.
The council's own original staff also provided a nucleus around which an increased organization could grow and function. The demands for research increased steadily until this staff increased fourfold, and the council was operating nine stations, in addition to its large central laboratory, either independently or in cooperation with the services.
The foregoing indicates briefly the means -by which the peace-time organization of associate committees and grants in aid of research were modified in order to meet the conditions of hurry and stress, and 'how the council staff provided a nucleus for the rapid development necessary. That the scholarships of the council have also proved their worth during this period is indicated by the fact that a large proportion of the young research men engaged in these [DOT]problems, either in civilian laboratories or in the services, have at one time held national research council scholarships, for post graduate training in science.
So far we have been dealing with internal coordination and cooperation. But facilities for the exchange of scientific information between Great Britain and the United States on the one hand, and Canada on the other, became very necessary. A new liaison organization was therefore developed to function as a channel for the exchange of confidential and secret information. The council maintains a chief scientific liaison officer in London, who supervises and expedites the exchanges between Great Britain and Canada; and exchanges between the United States and Canada are carried on through the Ottawa office. The liaison offices obtain and transmit scientific information not only for staff of the council but for other departments and for the armed forces.
Turning to the research work proper it might be well at the outset to indicate that while the importance of physical sciences in warfare is obvious, the country which would depend on these alone would be severely handicapped. The importance of such apparently insignificant items as insects and fungi may be overlooked by the uninitiated, but those responsible for maintaining the health of the troops and for the supply and storage of equipment in the field are acutely aware of their importance. For this reason work in many fields of applied biology has had to be speeded up.
The war-time history of the associated committee on medical research, which has already been mentioned, illustrates this fact. This committee has had to organize three specialist groups, one on aviation medical research under Dr. Duncan Graham, one on naval medical research under Surgeon Captain C. H. Best, and one on medical research for the army under Lt. Col. W. Hurst Brown.
The committee on aviation medical research has been responsible for an outstanding programme of work especially in the fields of high altitude flying, protective clothing for flyers, oxygen equipment, and personnel selection. Most of the flying clothing and auxiliary equipment developed by this committee is now in use in active combat. The committee has also been able to assist in the solution of medical and physiological problems that arose from new conditions encountered in service flying.
The committee on naval medical research works in close conjunction with the medical unit of the Royal Canadian Navy. Dietary surveys made by these groups resulted in recommendations for the correction of various dietary deficiencies. Attention has also been given to the quality of the rations and water carried on lifeboats. This committee has also concerned itself with the question of night vision, and tests which it developed for the evaluation of night vision, colour vision and visual acuity have been adopted by the navy. Special lighting techniques have been designed for use on bridge controls, bridge instruments and chart tables in order to minimize interference with night vision. In connection with the operation of anti-submarine detection devices, experimental work on the fatigue of personnel has yielded information which has been applied in determining the optimum length of watch periods. Tests designed to indicate personnel suitable for this branch of the service have been adopted by the Royal Canadian Navy, the Royal Navy and the United States navy. Investigations on such problems as "immersion foot", underwater blast injury, and eye protection for bridge and look-out personnel have produced satisfactory practical results.
At present further problems under investigation are: obtaining fresh water from sea water in life boats, protecting naval personnel from noise, combating fatigue in radio detector and wireless telegraph operators, following tracer bullets fired "into the sun", improving ventilation and lighting aboard ships, and healing and treatment of burns and shock.
The operation of large numbers of small vessels makes sea sickness a problem of special importance. In this connection groups working in Montreal and Toronto have devised techniques for sorting out those who are susceptible to motion sickness, and therapeutic measures have been devised to prevent or alleviate the condition in a large proportion of the cases tested.
Army medical research investigations are in progress on night vision, effort syndrome, evacuation of wounded from battlefields, the prevention of respiratory and other infections in barracks, the use of drugs in relation to motion sickness and gastric physiology, air ambulance transportation, fumigants, and water purification. In connection with nutrition, surveys have been made and a study of sprouted grains and legumes as sources of vitamins for troops is also under way.
In the council's division of applied biology, investigations on food problems not related to the war effort were dropped at the beginning of the war, and a pre-war staff of nine had to be increased to twenty-nine in order to cope with food problems referred to the council by various government departments.
The general programme of this division in connection with food has had to do largely with such products as jrork, bacon and eggs and in addition a large refrigeration project has been carried on. At the beginning of the war there was a shortage of refrigerated space and it became necessary to devise, if possible, a method of using the uninsulated holds of cargo vessels for the transportation of perishable products.
. Excellent progress has been made in the development of comparatively inexpensive emergency refrigeration equipment for this purpose which is easily and quickly installed, and which has
